paragraphs: Transoft Solutions makes software for the people who plan, design and operate transportation systems. Its work spans aviation, civil infrastructure, transportation and operational professionals. On the aviation side that means specialized software to plan, analyze and optimize airport and airspace operations.

The company started in 1991, when co-founder Milton Carrasco developed a vehicle tracking program called AutoTURN. That product grew out of his master's thesis on computerized vehicle-turning simulation. The range has widened since through in-house development and strategic acquisitions. One executive is credited with merging AeroTURN and PathPlanner into AviPLAN.

The company reports more than 100,000 customers in over 150 countries. Clients are described as government agencies at the federal, state, county and municipal levels, along with major international airports and engineering and architectural design firms. Headquarters are in British Columbia, Canada, with further offices in the United States, Australia, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Belgium, Germany, France, Sweden, Spain, India and China.

before.name: AirportLabs
before.description: Airport data platform, FIDS and operations apps for airport operators

paragraphs: AirportLabs sells hosted software that airports run their operations on, offered as one platform meant to address every facet of airport operations. The company describes its portfolio as a composable suite of operational products developed entirely in-house.

At the core is an airport operational database that unifies data streams so routine operations can be automated. Underneath it sits a data integration and API platform for aviation, built to be scalable and fault tolerant. Other products cover queue management, which the company says is built to optimise airport passenger flow. Aeronautical and commercial billing is handled by a product intended to automate core financial operations. A mobile community app gives airport teams a place to stay connected, resolve issues and keep operations running around the clock.

The site says more than 100 airports worldwide use its products. A customer success team is described as providing round-the-clock technical expertise and proactive health monitoring. Announcements on the site include a partnership with Cologne Bonn Airport to connect staff and centralise operations.

before.name: Aira
before.description: Visual interpreting accessibility service sponsored by airports and agencies

paragraphs: Aira runs a service that connects people who are blind or low-vision to professional visual interpreters for access to visual information. Remote video interpreting supports greater independence and communication for both the blind and low-vision community and the Deaf and hard-of-hearing community.

In the Explorer app, interpreters convey visual information verbally so that tasks become easier to accomplish. A second app, Aira ASL, connects a user to a professional ASL interpreter over live video with the option of real-time captioning. Explorer can be used at no cost at thousands of Access Partner locations worldwide. The ASL app is free at select Access Partner locations throughout North America.

Organizations that value accessibility partner with Aira to offer the service at no cost to their employees, students, or customers. Those partnerships cover accommodations for employees, Access programs for customers, and accessibility for digital and physical spaces. The company employs its own team of visual interpreters and recruits for those roles. A banner notes recognition on the Forbes Accessibility 200 List.

paragraphs: CLEAR sells an annual membership that verifies a traveler's identity and moves them through dedicated airport security lanes. The company describes itself more broadly as an identity business rather than an airport one.

Members can add up to three other people to an account, and CLEAR also handles enrollment and renewal for TSA PreCheck. An app is meant to cover the rest of the travel day, telling a member when to leave home to reach the gate on time. The same verification is offered away from airports, including entry at sports stadiums and arenas by showing a QR code in the app. A business-facing line called CLEAR1 extends the identity checks to enterprises.

Caryn Seidman Becker is the Chair, CEO and Founder. The company says she acquired CLEAR out of bankruptcy in 2010 and grew it to 62 airport locations, hundreds of partners and more than 43 million verified users nationwide.

before.name: RunwayStats
before.description: Real-time airport operations tracking and traffic-count analytics with noise complaint investigation and FAA funding-ready reporting for GA and commercial airports.

paragraphs: RunwayStats sells an airport traffic tracking system built on a receiver placed on the airfield and a dashboard, so that every aircraft touching the airport is counted, identified, and stored. Every takeoff, landing, touch and go, go around, helicopter operation, and airspace transition at the airport is detected automatically and logged in real time. Each logged operation carries the time, registration, callsign, runway used, weather conditions, aircraft make and model, and owner, and the data can be filtered, searched, and downloaded to CSV.

Reports run for any day, month, or year on demand or on a schedule, with delivery to an inbox, a board, or a state DOT. Noise complaints are handled by a complaint management add on that logs, investigates, and tracks each complaint through resolution. A separate add on covers commercial operations, tracking scheduled, estimated, and actual times for arrivals and departures along with on-time performance, gate usage, and taxi times.

Multiple Airports is built for engineering firms, counties, port authorities, and airport groups with more than one airport under their wing. Subscriptions are sold in Essentials and Platinum tiers, and features from any tier can be mixed into one package.

before.name: GoApron, Inc.
before.description: Cloud platform that digitizes apron and gate operations: aircraft parking assignment, scheduling, utilization forecasting and aeronautical revenue capture. - exhibited at AAAE 2027

paragraphs: GoApron sells cloud-based software that airports use to automate gate utilization, aircraft parking, and the rates and charges attached to them. The airlines and ground handlers that share the apron work in the same system, requesting gates and remote spots instead of phoning or emailing for them. It is meant to be used away from a desk as well as at one.

Gates and aircraft parking spots are assigned in advance or on demand, and usage is tracked through automated scheduling. Gate and remote parking schedules can be viewed and changed in real time. The same records feed billing, with monthly airline charges calculated and reconciled from actual per-turn use. Landings that previously went uncaptured are recorded, along with landing weight totals and RON tracking.

The company describes an industry where planes are still parked using pen, paper, fax, spreadsheets and PDFs. Airfield operations specialists, it says, lose day and night shift hours to calls from airlines and ground handlers. GoApron says it offers airline partners gates and spots based on preferential use, aircraft size, operational rules and real-time data.

before.name: Assaia International
before.description: Computer-vision turnaround and apron monitoring for airports and airlines

paragraphs: Assaia sells software that gives airports, airlines, and ground handlers real-time visibility into aircraft turnaround operations. The problem it names is that missing visibility on the ramp produces costly delays, underutilized capacity, miscommunication, accidents, missed service level agreements, and excess emissions.

Cameras placed across aircraft stands, aerobridges, and the apron generate accurate timestamps for turnaround events in real time. Machine-learning models turn those timestamps into predictions for aircraft off-block and departure readiness. The company says the system can use a wide range of cameras already installed at airports around the world. It runs in the cloud and on premise.

Beyond the core product, SafetyControl detects unsafe situations on the ramp for airports, airlines, and ground handlers. EmissionsControl gives airports real-time monitoring of auxiliary power unit engine usage. A separate interface is designed for airline users, ground handlers, departure coordinators, and gate managers. The company names JFKIAT and Seattle-Tacoma among the airports where its apron product has been deployed. It also states that the solution is fully compliant with the General Data Protection Regulation.

paragraphs: Senstar makes security systems for protecting infrastructure and facilities. The portfolio runs across video management, video analytics, access control and perimeter intrusion detection sensors. Products are designed, manufactured and tested in North America.

Perimeter sensors mount on the fence, sit above ground or lie buried, and are meant to locate intruders before they enter a secure area. The MultiSensor unit packs short-range radar, an image sensor, dual PIR, an accelerometer and a high frequency sensor into one device. An embedded engine weighs the data from each of those sensors to decide whether an event is a threat. On the software side, Senstar Symphony is a modular platform for security management and data intelligence. It works with analog and IP cameras, encoders, DVRs and other video devices from many manufacturers.

The company organizes its work by sector, pointing to electrical utility assets exposed to service interruptions from vandalism, theft and targeted attacks. Water treatment plants, pumping stations and storage tanks are another market it names. It states over 40 years of experience working with correctional institutions. before.name: AirGarage
before.description: Full-service automated parking operations for cities and airports

paragraphs: AirGarage runs the parking lots and garages that sit on other people's real estate, managing them for the owner. Instead of selling equipment or a booking app on its own, the company takes on the hardware, the software and the daily operations together.

Cameras on site gather data in real time, and dashboards turn that into a picture of how the property is performing. Rates then move automatically with the market rather than sitting at a fixed posted price. Enforcement is handled by staff on the ground, backed by LPR and aerial camera technology. The company also markets each lot to drivers on the parking aggregator sites they already use. Owners are billed through a revenue share rather than a flat management fee. Agreements run month to month rather than on a long term contract.

AirGarage started in 2017. It says it now partners with hundreds of properties nationwide, from independent owners to institutional investors. Its published case studies include 75 Saint, a 185-space lot and garage in Boston owned by Jefferson Apartment Group. The about page also lists news coverage of a $12.5M round led by a16z.

before.name: Outsight SA
before.location: Paris, France (offices in San Francisco and Singapore)
before.description: LiDAR-based spatial intelligence software turning 3D sensor data into anonymous passenger flow, queue wait time and occupancy analytics for terminals and curbside.

paragraphs: Outsight sells software that turns 3D sensor feeds into a running account of how people, vehicles, and robots move through a site. The buyers are operators of large shared spaces such as airports, hospitals, and factories.

Anything entering the scene is given an anonymous identifier and held to centimeter precision until it leaves. No faces or plates are captured, only the geometry of motion. Operators define zones and the measures they care about, such as counting, density, queue length, wait time and throughput, and the analytics engine computes them continuously. Results come back as live 3D playback, custom indicators, alerts, dashboards, and APIs. Before any of that, a multi-vendor simulator tests layouts and sensor mixes and proposes the hardware configuration.

The company says the platform is deployed at scale across five continents. It calls the result a Motional Digital Twin and says these are running in production. Its newsroom announces a strategic partnership with AWS around spatial AI in aviation. The pitch behind all of it is that movement is the next layer of business to be digitized.

quote.text: The bottleneck of Physical AI is not models, it is real-world data

provenance.quote: An end-to-end software solution combining Physical AI, multi-sensor fusion, and real-time analytics to continuously digitize the movement of people, vehicles, and robots across entire sites.

paragraphs: Outsight sells software that turns 3D sensor feeds into a running account of how people, vehicles, and robots move through a site. The buyers are operators of large shared spaces such as airports, hospitals, and factories.

Anything entering the scene is given an anonymous identifier and held to centimeter precision until it leaves. No faces or plates are captured, only the geometry of motion. Operators define zones and the measures they care about, such as counting, density, queue length, wait time and throughput, and the analytics engine computes them continuously. Results come back as live 3D playback, custom indicators, alerts, dashboards, and APIs. before.name: Dedrone by Axon
before.description: Airspace security and drone detection for airports and public agencies

paragraphs: Dedrone by Axon sells counter-drone systems that secure fixed locations such as airports, correctional facilities and critical infrastructure from unauthorized drones. Law enforcement, military and public safety organizations are named as the buyers for its mobile unit.

A fixed installation combines radio-frequency sensors, radar and pan-tilt-zoom cameras over the airspace at a site. The radio-frequency sensors analyse signals to detect and locate both the drone and its pilot. Cameras add visual verification of a drone incursion. Command and control software called DedroneTracker.AI fuses those tracks and reports drone and pilot location. A towable trailer packages the same mix for temporary sites and is described as set up in less than twenty minutes. A city-wide option skips installed equipment altogether, letting users mark alert zones and get notified when drones enter them.

The company states that its fixed-site product is deployed at over 829 sites globally. It says its customers include military organizations, airports, correctional facilities, stadiums and critical infrastructure sites. The city-wide app is described as available in over 50 cities.

before.name: Copenhagen Optimization
before.description: Better Airport forecasting and capacity planning for airport terminals

paragraphs: Copenhagen Optimization sells planning software and consulting to airports that are running into capacity limits in their terminals. Its platform, Better Airport, is a cloud-based system for running core operations such as check-in, baggage, security, stand and gate, and immigration.

The company says the platform ties together operations that were once run separately, so data can move between them. Consulting sits alongside the software and draws on operational strategy, analytics, planning and optimization. Individual modules cover forecasting, security and shift planning.

Case studies describe Sydney Airport adopting the suite with two modules and later extending one of them across all terminals. At Manchester Airport, a rostering project cut the security roster count from more than 60 to 10. Heathrow Airport Limited commissioned an assessment of planning maturity across 15 operational areas. The company dates its airport work to 2014.

before.name: UVeye
before.description: Automated vehicle inspection portals for airports, borders and government

paragraphs: UVeye builds automated inspection systems that scan the full exterior, undercarriage, and tires of a vehicle in seconds. Dealerships use the scans to document pre-existing damage and avoid unnecessary claims. Seaports and logistics hubs use touchless inspections to speed vehicle handoffs and settle disputes. Bus and truck operators run standardized inspections to improve compliance.

A scan combines high-resolution imaging, sensors, and patented AI to surface problems the eye cannot catch. Findings run from tire wear and misalignment to leaks, rust, and underbody damage. Output arrives as images and measurements of dents, scratches, and undercarriage issues. Automatic notifications flag critical issues that need immediate attention.

Brothers Amir and Ohad Hever founded UVeye in 2016. The first application was undercarriage security screening, which grew into a platform that scans whole vehicles. Systems are now deployed across hundreds of dealerships, fleets, rental agencies, and manufacturing lines worldwide. The company names Amazon, General Motors, Volvo, and CarMax among the companies using it. It reports over $380 million raised.

paragraphs: Pointr sells indoor mapping and wayfinding software that turns a venue, office or campus into interactive digital maps. Customers put those maps into their own apps, on the web, or on kiosks, using dedicated mobile and web SDKs. One stated use is guiding travelers to their gate with turn-by-turn updates and estimated arrival times.

Maps are generated from CAD files by an AI tool called MapScale. Blue dot positioning indoors runs on Bluetooth Low Energy rather than a satellite signal. The site says accuracy holds without fingerprinting or geomagnetism, so the system needs less ongoing maintenance. Geofences drawn on the map trigger actions when visitors enter or leave a zone.

The company describes itself as the top choice for Fortune 100 companies. Its homepage names product wayfinding work at The Home Depot. It states that its positioning technology is patented, with more than ten years of testing and development behind it. On privacy, the geofencing page says visitor location data is collected anonymously and aligned with GDPR.

paragraphs: AeroCloud Systems sells cloud-based airport management software that airport teams use to run daily operations. Three lines make up the offer: an airport operations system, passenger processing, and passenger flow monitoring under the name AeroCloud Optic.

The operations system is modular, so an airport pays for the pieces it needs and adds more later. before.name: Liberty Defense
before.description: HEXWAVE walk-through concealed weapons detection plus body and shoe scanners for aviation checkpoints and public venues. - exhibited at ACA Congress 2026

paragraphs: Liberty Defense makes AI-based detection equipment for finding concealed weapons and other threats in urban security and aviation settings. Its main product, HEXWAVE, is a walkthrough portal that screens for nonmetallic and metallic threats without asking people to remove shoes, jewelry, belts or jackets.

It uses active millimeter wave, video-rate 3D imaging and AI to detect concealed metallic and non-metallic weapons and other prohibited items. The company says the imaging captures over 400,000 voxels. No images are stored, and none are accessible by the security operator. The operator sees only a go or no-go screen with a clear alert. For aviation, Liberty holds exclusive licenses to two solutions developed by PNNL and funded by the Department of Homeland Security.

The home page states that Liberty delivers HEXWAVE to the TSA. It also says the company is developing screening for aviation workers. Named settings include hotels, schools, airports, public transit systems, places of religion and entertainment venues. On its finances, the company reports completing an initial public offering in the United States that raised approximately $20 million in gross proceeds.

before.name: FLASH
before.description: Cloud parking OS and reservations for airports, cities and venues

paragraphs: Flash sells parking technology that connects asset owners, operators and drivers through software, hardware and demand channels. It says the platform is implemented across hotels, airports, municipalities, new construction and higher education.

Drivers reserve through the apps, ticket platforms and vehicle interfaces they already use. Camera-based access lets them enter and exit without stopping at a barrier. Express Pay, powered by Vision AI cameras, delivers automated ticketless parking. Enrollment for that happens once through ParkMobile or ParkWhiz. EV charging sits in the same flow, so drivers locate, reserve and pay for charging alongside parking. A valet product lets customers text to request their car.

The company's own timeline says the business was founded as Klever Logic. The same timeline records a $250M investment from Vista Equity Partners. It also records a merger between Flash and Arrive. Support runs through a network of regional offices and field technicians. One highlighted result points to work completed in 22 days at Denver International Airport.

before.description: Bird-strike avoidance radar and wildlife management systems for airports

paragraphs: DeTect, Inc builds 2D and True3D radar and related remote sensing systems for aviation safety, security and surveillance, drone defense and environmental protection. The company describes itself as the leader in bird radar for real-time aircraft bird strike avoidance, wind energy bird mortality risk assessment and industrial bird control.

The signal processing developed for its MERLIN bird radar also runs in the HARRIER security and surveillance radar and the DroneWatcher drone detection radars. Each system is sold with turn-key delivery and installation, concept-of-operations development, user training and long-term 24-7 remote and on-site service.

DeTect says it has offices, engineering and manufacturing space in Canada, Poland, South Korea, the UK and US. It counts over 20,000 square feet of office, laboratory and manufacturing space in Florida, Poland and South Korea. The company states that the U.S. Department of Defense has purchased twenty MERLIN systems to date. It also states that NASA selected the MERLIN system in 2006 to support space launch safety.

before.name: Gallagher Security
before.description: Access control and perimeter security for airports and critical government sites

paragraphs: Gallagher Security designs and manufactures integrated security products across access control, perimeter security, intruder alarms, and cybersecurity. Its customers range from small businesses to enterprise organizations and critical infrastructure sites. Systems are sized from a single door to thousands across multiple sites.

Access control runs on card readers, mobile credentials, and biometric devices that verify permissions. Controllers act as the central hub, processing access requests and communicating with connected systems. Roles, schedules, and activity are managed in Command Centre, the company's centralized platform, with customizable dashboards and reporting. On the perimeter, high-tensile pulse fences form a visual barrier and deliver safe, short pulses that deter intruders. Sensors alert a team the moment a fence is touched. Perimeter protection is a native part of Command Centre, the same software that runs access control and intruder detection. It works with most existing fence types, so a site can add detection without replacing its fencing.

The company says it has been doing this work for over 35 years. Listed uses include safeguarding energy plants, utilities, airports, and seaports with multi-layered systems. Another is securing classified areas and complying with defense standards. Published case studies include one on the Indiana Department of Corrections. A featured project spans campus life for students and staff across 143 buildings and 150 research centres.

paragraphs: IER presents itself as a supplier working alongside public and private organizations. The stated work is connecting and automating the movement of passengers and of goods.

Each container carries an RFID tag with a QR code, so it can be identified and its states and locations traced. On the airport side the site presents Skycheck from EASIER, a self-service check-in kiosk. It lets travelers check themselves in and print boarding passes and baggage tags. The kiosk is described as compatible with CUSS 1.5 and 2.0 and with biometrics, in a fixed or battery-powered portable version.

The company describes its own strength as expertise in technology, production and integration for demanding operating environments. Service coverage is described as worldwide, supported by many locations. Support is delivered either by IER subsidiaries or through a network of selected local partners.

before.name: 33 ALERTS
before.description: QR-code-based emergency alerting system: travelers or staff scan a placarded decal to report an incident and security/ops teams instantly receive the alert with exact location, no app download required. - exhibited at AAAE 2027

paragraphs: 33 ALERTS sells printed QR code decals that let the people inside a venue report a problem by scanning a code with a phone camera. Reports range from facility complaints to suspicious activity, and the site is explicit that the service is not a replacement for 911.

A person opens the phone camera and scans the decal, with no download or account required. That sends a text message to the venue security operations center or response team carrying the exact location where help is needed. The receiving team can message the reporter back to ask questions. In arenas the placement is described down to section, row and seat.

Settings named on the site include colleges, universities and PK-12 schools, alongside stadiums, fairs, parks and airports. On campuses the decals are pitched as reaching places blue light emergency phones do not. The page carries a copyright notice for 33 Systems Inc., doing business as 33 ALERTS, of Tampa, Florida.

paragraphs: EnSight Technologies sells parking technology built around occupancy counting, parking guidance, vehicle identification, and paid parker management. before.name: QLess, Inc.
before.description: Virtual queuing and appointment scheduling SaaS used by airports and government agencies to eliminate physical lines at badging offices and service counters.

paragraphs: QLESS sells queue management software that lets an organization replace a physical line with a virtual one. Customers join a wait list from a phone or the web and get a notification when their turn comes. The platform also books appointments, sends reminders, and offers open slots to other customers after a cancellation.

Walk-ins, appointments, virtual visits and callbacks run through one system rather than separate tools. Managers watch throughput in real time, see where the backlog sits, and survey customers after a visit. Locations can be shut down or appointments redirected, with customers notified by SMS or email.

Qless describes the buyers as organizations across government, healthcare, higher education, retail and enterprise services. Ownership sits with Palisades Equity, a private investment firm. Security material on the site lists encryption of data in transit and at rest and role based access controls.

before.name: The Weather Company

paragraphs: The Weather Company sells weather data, forecasting, and insights to consumers and businesses alike. The industries it names are advertising, aviation, media, and government.

Much of the business runs through a weather data API that customers fold into their own applications, business processes, or custom models. For aviation the pitch is converting complex meteorological data into decision-ready flight and ground insights. The stated aim there is fewer costly delays, better fuel use, and safer crews and passengers from preflight to touchdown. A separate government and defense line is aimed at mission risk from command centers to the tactical edge.

The company traces its work back nearly five decades, combining human meteorological expertise with technology. It also powers a portfolio of three consumer brands used daily around the world. Case studies describe Breeze Airways using its Fusion flight tracking to run more efficiently through major weather events and resume operations faster after disruptions. Another describes NASCAR unifying its weather intelligence with the company to make scheduling and safety calls.

paragraphs: HUB Parking Technology develops, manufactures, installs and services smart parking systems, and handles after-sales support for them. It is the brand of FAAC Technologies dedicated to the parking and mobility industries. Its customers are operators running anything from single facilities to global networks.

Jupiter is built to adapt to systems using license plate recognition, contract parking, credit card in and out parking, or online pre-paid parking. before.name: Hidden Level
before.description: Passive airspace monitoring sensors for airports and government agencies

paragraphs: Hidden Level sells radio-frequency sensing hardware and data services to government, defense and commercial security teams. The sensing is passive, which the company says leaves the equipment undetected and hard to jam.

The Breaker sensor is built for fixed sites and is meant to coexist with infrastructure and telecom equipment already there. The Surge mounts to land and water vehicles and is made to withstand harsh conditions. Customers who would rather not run hardware can buy data from a global sensor network the company owns, operates and maintains. That service pinpoints drone operator location and lets users define zones so alerts arrive only for activity in chosen areas. Data reaches other systems through an open API secured with FIPS 140-2 compliant cryptography, or through a web interface.

Stated uses include protecting airspace around stadiums, airports and buildings, and preventing contraband drone deliveries to correctional facilities. The hardware page cites FCC compliance along with TRL9 and MIL-STD-810 testing. The company says its sensors analyze the physical characteristics of signals without decoding private information. Researchers can reach the collected captures through APIs for training and benchmarking work.

before.name: AirBadge
before.description: Cloud identity management system (IDMS) purpose-built for US airport badge offices: applications, renewals, TSA audit compliance, training and scheduling, integrated with fingerprint, PACS (LenelS2) and training platforms. - exhibited at AAAE 2027

paragraphs: AirBadge sells identity management software to airports in the United States, aimed at the badge office that issues and renews credentials. The company says it puts all of its resources into aviation so the software fits airport operations and TSA regulations. The product is described as built for 1542 and part 139 airports.

Applicants and badge holders enter their own details into the system. Those details are then sent directly to integrated systems, which removes a round of rekeying. It automates badge applications, appointment scheduling, training and testing, and cuts manual entry at fingerprinting, physical access control and TSC. Authorized signatories use it to invite new hires to apply and to authorize or block renewals. It runs on fully managed cloud infrastructure.

The site says more than 50 airports in the United States use it. It presents itself as a fit for airports of any size. The company announced LenelS2 factory certification and membership in the LenelS2 OpenAccess Alliance Program. Its software interfaces with the LenelS2 OnGuard access control system. Deployment is pitched in weeks rather than years.

before.name: FlightBI
before.description: AI-powered aviation data warehouse and business intelligence apps (Fligence suite) for airports, airlines and route/catchment analysis.

paragraphs: FlightBI sells aviation business intelligence to airports, helping their managers read flight distribution, demand growth, traffic origins and destinations, and traveler behavior. It sells to airlines as well, covering market size, demand growth, fare trends and the competitive landscape. Travel management companies are a third audience, using the analysis to read traveler preferences and behavior.

The products are sold as a suite for aviation decision making. One platform analyzes passenger origins at ZIP-code level and measures traffic leakage to competing airports. A separate catchment platform works at the census subdivision level for Canadian airports. A planning platform helps air service development teams find market opportunities and build airline proposals. before.name: Elenium Automation
before.description: Touchless self-service check-in and bag drop technology for airports

paragraphs: Elenium Automation makes self-service check-in kiosks and bag drops for airports and airlines. The company describes bag drops that cut queues and keep passengers moving through the terminal. It pitches the same equipment to airlines as a way of activating their services instantly at any airport.

The product suite is called VYGR, short for Voyager, and covers self-service steps of the passenger journey. Elenium says it is built on computer vision, AI, modern UX, and a cloud backbone. The company reports achieving over 97% first-time read rates and sub-15 second processing speeds on its bag drop. In 2020 it launched HealthGate, described as an automated, touchless fever detection device approved by both the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration and the European Medicines Agency. The company also says it achieved ISO 13485 certification.

Elenium was founded in 2015 by Aaron Hornlimann, Fred Melki, and Heinz Corona. It says it now operates in over 35 airports, serving more than 45 airlines and 250 million passengers annually across Australasia, Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East, Europe, and the UK. For service, the company describes partnering with Unisys to provide global 24 by 7, remote and onsite support coverage.

before.name: Agents of Discovery
before.description: Mobile augmented-reality game platform licensed to airports, parks and public agencies to engage visitors with location-triggered educational missions and wayfinding-style content. - exhibited at Washington Recreation and Park Association 2026
before.source: AAAE 2026; Washington Recreation and Park Association 2026

paragraphs: Agents of Discovery turns physical spaces such as museums, airports, campuses, libraries, stadiums and entire cities into interactive learning environments by blending AI-driven content generation with place-based augmented reality gameplay. Customers become what the company calls Mission Makers, turning their own stories, spaces and content into augmented reality experiences.

Location-based challenges are placed on site and tied to the customer's own content, or played from anywhere. A site can also deploy a fully customized AI avatar as its on-site guide. Self-guided tours are offered around the clock. Exhibits can be built for aquariums, zoos and museums. Text-to-speech and multiple language options are meant to keep the platform reachable for players with diverse abilities and backgrounds.

Airports are one named setting, where the pitch is turning downtime into interactive adventures built for travelers. Junior Ranger Missions on the platform cover subjects from palaeontology and fossils to International Migratory Bird Day. The chief academic officer works with public and private organizations across the United States, Australia and Canada on visitor experience. The company describes itself as a Harvard-incubated AI and augmented reality company.

before.name: Cleverciti
before.description: Overhead parking occupancy sensing and guidance for airports and cities

paragraphs: Cleverciti sells outdoor and on-street parking detection, monitoring and guidance systems. The company describes its work as applying integrated technology to parking, congestion and compliance problems using real-time occupancy and payment data. Deployments span retail, smart city, entertainment, education and transportation settings. Airports are one target, where the pitch is winning back customers from off-airport parking.

Digital signage placed at each intersection and parking aisle entrance keeps drivers from circling or driving into fully occupied areas. The displays are meant to blend into the existing streetscape, wrapping around lampposts. Occupancy data can be published to any other system through a REST API. Rather than launching another app, availability, search and guidance components can be built into an app visitors already use. Fully digital 360 degree displays can push updated messaging visible from all directions.

Cleverciti was founded in 2012 by Thomas Hohenacker and Konrad Prinz-Dreher. It reports deployments at over 200 locations in over 20 countries. Offices include European headquarters in Munich, Germany, and North American headquarters in Atlanta. Among the projects it describes, the company says it led an on-street guidance deployment in Cologne and supplied the hardware and software to RheinEnergie, the city utility company.

paragraphs: Tadera sells airport software, and its staff includes former airport leaders along with subject matter experts in security, accounting, safety, and human resources. The finance tools are aimed at airports and systems of airports, covering property management, contracts, lease terms, billing, receivable and reporting, as well as capital improvement programs. A separate Secure Credentials product handles biometric credentialing, badging, continuous vetting, auditing, and access management, and helps meet TSA security directives.

ABRM, the Airport Business and Revenue Manager, consolidates lease management, billing, revenue tracking, tenant communications, and financial reporting into one system, covering both aeronautical and non-aeronautical revenue streams. It supports lease terms including minimum annual guarantees, fixed rent escalations, CPIs, ceilings, and floors, and tracks lease data elements for GASB 87 compliance.

Airport Project Manager covers capital programs, with an AIP Management Module tracking applications, funding, and compliance for FAA, FEMA, and state and local grants. Airport System Manager is built for state departments of transportation, combining grant tracking, facility inspections, aircraft registration, licensing, project funding, and data analysis into one application.

paragraphs: Zensors sells AI meant to automate processes in the physical world, between people, buildings and machines. It describes itself as an AI company building multimodal physical AI that learns to perceive the world with human level accuracy.

The system ingests data from sensors, cameras and other devices and merges it with text and metadata from data warehouses into one aligned format. Models then run across video, time-series and text to build an understanding of a space and the activity inside it. On top of that sit agents intended to automate operational decisions rather than only report them. The company says its models arrive pre-trained on billions of images, videos and text specific to each vertical, so no extensive retraining is required. It also says output is written for IT, operations and business stakeholders while individual customers stay anonymous.

The models are sold as industry-specific and pre-trained for particular kinds of large, complex spaces. Airports are one of the settings its published guidance addresses. The company was spun out of Carnegie Mellon University. Its stated mission is to let anyone create and manage AI without a doctorate in machine learning. Its leadership page describes a head of product and technology steering the system toward suggesting actions that optimize operations.

before.name: Alcatraz
before.description: Alcatraz AI Rock: 3D facial authentication and tailgating detection device that replaces or augments badge readers at secure doors, integrating with existing access control systems.

paragraphs: Alcatraz makes facial authentication products that work with the badge readers and access control systems an organization already runs. The device, called Rock X, sits in line between the badge reader and the access control panel over Wiegand or OSDP.

Employees enroll at a station, remotely from a browser or phone, or automatically after repeated badge swipes at a door fitted with the device. Authentication happens on the device itself, and the company states that no sensitive data is stored or transmitted. Profiles are anonymized and tied to the badge ID already held in the customer's access control system. The same unit can act as a passive second factor, so a person badges in as usual and the face confirms the match. In lobbies it can be built directly into certain turnstiles. The management platform runs on premise or in the cloud.

Airports are one setting the company writes about, pairing face recognition with badges or PINs to add a second factor at restricted doors. One unnamed case summary on the site describes a global enterprise that put the device on turnstiles for more than 150,000 employees. The company says its approach helps customers conform with privacy regulations such as BIPA, CCPA and GDPR.

before.name: Neighborly Software
before.description: Grant and program administration software for affordable housing, disaster recovery, vouchers and energy rebate programs run by local and state agencies - exhibited at NAHRO 2026, NCSHA 2026

paragraphs: Neighborly Software sells a cloud platform for administering and disbursing government funds. It connects administrators, participants, contractors and homeowners in one system for local, state and nonprofit organizations.

The programs covered include housing, economic and community development, disaster recovery and mitigation, home energy rebates, and housing choice vouchers. Community development activity runs from application to closeout on a single platform. Integration with the IDIS reporting system is meant to end duplicate data entry. For disaster recovery grants, the company says it implements in weeks rather than months.

The company says more than a third of HUD entitlement jurisdictions choose it. Published case studies include Prince William County, Virginia. It dates to 2016 and says it has delivered software to more than 700 public and private sector entities across the country. Co-founder and president Jason Rusnak previously held management positions at Accenture and ADP.

paragraphs: Localintel sells an AI-powered platform that turns data about a community into charts, maps, dashboards, stories, reports, and website embeds. The catalog includes formatted reports on economy, workforce, housing, demographics, and quality of life, exportable as PDFs or share web links. It also produces plain-language narratives that explain what the data means, editable in Word for newsletters, reports, blogs, and board packs.

A separate products page lists interactive data visualization tools that a customer embeds on a website to show a location's strengths. One of those tools helps businesses find commercial properties that are currently for sale or lease. Another shows the universities and colleges supplying talent to businesses in a location.

The pages present the platform to public-sector teams in economic development, planning, communications, parks and recreation, public works, grants, finance, and IT. A case study names Norfolk County, whose team published a data-rich news article in its first week with the platform. The about page says hundreds of communities across the US and Canada use Localintel products.

quote.text: Ready-to-publish location content for government teams

paragraphs: AffordableHousing.com runs an online rental marketplace for people looking for low income, subsidized and Section 8 housing. The company calls itself the largest online marketplace for affordable housing in the country.

Registration is free for renters and opens up listing details, online applications, waiting list updates, saved searches and new listing alerts. On the other side, property owners post units to reach renters and the housing agencies that support them. Reference pages explain that Section 8, also called the Housing Choice Voucher program, covers part of a renter's monthly rent. Other pages point renters to the local housing authorities that review applications, check eligibility and issue vouchers.

The company says its partnerships since 2003 include HUD, thousands of government agencies and property owners nationwide. It states that housing agencies have partnered with it since 2005. The site publishes reviews from renters and property managers alongside its listings.

paragraphs: HousingOS is program administration software built for municipal housing teams. The company positions it as a way for housing departments to manage CDBG, HOME, and local rehab funds in one place.

The system follows a case from application intake through construction management, loan servicing and yearly monitoring. Structured workflows guide users through each phase so that nothing is missed. Administrators assign database access based on staff roles. The software also generates email notices, monitoring letters, payoff requests and reconveyances from templates.

A companion online application portal feeds the system, with approved applications importing straight into HousingOS. The company says it builds this site with WCAG and Section 508 accessibility principles in mind. Pricing is quoted agency by agency, on the reasoning that every agency's programs are different.

paragraphs: PHA-Web is web-based software that provides tenant, property, and financial management to housing authorities across the United States. The software comes from Management Computer Services, Inc., which was founded in 1968 and by 1970 had dedicated its services to public housing authorities. Company pages put the reach of the software at over 800 agencies nationwide and at over 25 percent of the housing authority industry.

Tenant, property, and financial components are described as the core of the software. Portals for applicants, tenants, and landlords sit alongside those components. A Document Imaging component stores tenant, landlord, and vendor files. An Executive Dashboard presents key performance indicators, metrics, and reports for executive staff.
Feature work described on the site covers use from any mobile device, reduced paper usage, and reporting for executive staff members. The careers page describes the company as a small business.

before.name: Cognisen
before.description: AI report writing and field supervision assistant for probation, parole, and pretrial agencies - exhibited at APPA Probation 2026, ACA Congress 2026
before.source: conference sweep: APPA Probation 2026; ACA Congress 2026

paragraphs: Cognisen builds AI tools for probation, parole, and pretrial agencies, helping staff draft reports faster, capture case notes in the moment, and find answers across case files. The work it covers runs from pre-sentence investigations to field contacts.

Report writing software turns pre-sentence investigations, court reports, and case documentation into structured workflows built for the agency. A mobile app gives officers and agents what they need before, during, and after every visit, from the field. An assistant opens up case data, policies, and agency insights through secure conversation. The company says that assistant surfaces information and never creates decisions. Officers and agents review and approve every action before it becomes part of the record. The platform connects to an agency's existing system of record.

The company says agencies and departments use the software across their core workflows. The assistant is described as CJIS-compliant. Cognisen states that most agencies launch within 120 days. Rollout starts with a pilot group before expanding. It says the platform runs in a secure AWS GovCloud environment. The company also states that agency records are not used to train AI.

before.description: TrueFiling e-filing and digital workflow systems for courts and agencies

paragraphs: The company implements, extends and integrates Hyland OnBase content management for organizations whose work is buried in documents and cases. Its stated ground is complex environments, from court systems and departments of transportation to healthcare payers and utilities.

Document processing uses AI and machine learning to capture, classify, extract and validate data, which cuts manual keying. For courts and justice agencies the offering runs to case type specific workflows, eFiling and digital evidence management. A platform called Vault holds multimedia evidence, with device-agnostic playback, secure sharing and chain-of-custody tracking. paragraphs: SuperCom describes itself as a secure solutions integrator and technology provider for governments and other consumers facing organizations. Its offender products are grouped as a PureSecurity suite, which includes the PureTag RF bracelet for use across that suite. before.name: Casepoint
before.description: Cloud eDiscovery and legal hold platform for government agencies and courts

paragraphs: Casepoint sells a cloud platform for eDiscovery, FOIA, investigations, and compliance work. Inside it, teams collect, process, analyze, review, and produce data in one place. The pitch is that all the data for a matter is managed in one place rather than moved between tools.

Connectors pull data straight from platforms such as Slack, Microsoft 365, and Teams. The processing engine supports over 600 file types. A separate FOIA product is built around how agencies respond to public records requests. Requesters use a portal to file requests and pay for them through pay.gov. For Canada, ATIPXpress carries access and privacy requests from submission through search, review, redaction, exemption analysis, and delivery.

The company describes the platform as purpose-built for corporations and government entities. It states that Casepoint holds FedRAMP Moderate and High authorizations, ISO 27001 certification, and Department of Defense Impact Level 5 and Impact Level 6 authorizations. It also claims to be one of only six SaaS companies globally with DOD IL6 authorization. Its AI is described as built for legal and regulatory work.

before.name: For The Record (FTR)
before.description: Digital court recording and record management technology for judiciaries - exhibited at NACM 2026

paragraphs: For The Record makes recording technology for courts, capturing what is said in a proceeding and turning it into text that can be searched. One audience is court administrators trying to keep operations running at lower cost. Judges are a second audience, able to pull up audio, video, and speech-to-text without leaving the bench.

Recording runs on multiple audio channels, so individual speakers stay distinct even when they talk over one another. Courts that need local infrastructure can run the FTR Gold software in the courthouse rather than in the cloud. The cloud option is described as centralized storage built to NIST 800-53 Rev. 5 with more than a thousand security and privacy controls. Access is governed by role-based permissions, audit trails, and encryption of both transmission and storage.

The company says it supports courts in more than 80 countries. Its software is API-ready and meant to sit alongside the case management and evidence systems a court already runs. The work extends past software into specifying equipment and installing courtroom hardware.

before.name: JusticeText
before.description: AI evidence transcription and analysis (bodycam, interrogation) for public defenders and DAs

paragraphs: JusticeText sells evidence review software for criminal defense work, turning hours of audio and video discovery into searchable transcripts synced to the original media. The platform transcribes and translates media in more than 100 languages, including files where several languages are spoken. An assistant called MirandaAI works across every piece of evidence in a case to uncover connections. Attorneys can build case timelines, spot inconsistencies and flag key moments across the evidence.

Video clipping, redaction and closed captioning tools are offered for building court exhibits. Multiple camera angles can be synced into one timeline aligned by date and time of capture. Uploaded content is stored on encrypted servers in the United States, encrypted in transit and at rest. The product page states that evidence is never used to train third-party machine learning models. Account access is protected with multi-factor authentication and single sign-on support.

The buyers named on these pages are criminal defense teams, described as thousands of attorneys across the United States. The Kentucky Department of Public Advocacy brought on JusticeText in 2023 for digital evidence review. Harris County Public Defenders are described as drawing insights from large quantities of audiovisual evidence with it. Private defense practices appear as well, including Rossen Law Firm, whose founder uses it to review evidence and create exhibits for court.

before.name: DIMS
before.description: Case management, drug testing lab management and participant supervision software for treatment courts, probation and pretrial agencies - exhibited at APPA Probation 2026

paragraphs: DIMS sells case management software for specialty and treatment courts. It also sells cloud-based probation and pretrial software for managing clients, supervising cases and running risk assessments. Drug testing is the third piece, offered as one digital solution with laboratory information management for instrument or instant testing.

Participant data sits on a platform the company describes as HIPAA compliant, with visual analytics and reporting. The pieces are vertically integrated with case management, lab information systems and accounting platforms so that people and resources are not entered twice. A digital cup product is described as improving the accuracy of reported results and removing errors in data delivery. Alcohol testing runs through a portable breathalyzer paired to the client's phone over Bluetooth. Automated notifications remind participants to check in and submit a photo for verification. Each check-in carries a timestamp and geo-tag recording where the participant was at the moment of submission.

The company says courts in 46 states use the system. Versions are customized for different court types, from adult treatment courts to DUI courts. It states that there are no long term contracts. The product is presented as designed by justice professionals for treatment court needs.

before.name: Outreach Smartphone Monitoring
before.description: Smartphone-based GPS, breathalyzer, and check-in monitoring for probation and pretrial supervision agencies - exhibited at APPA Probation 2026

paragraphs: Outreach Smartphone Monitoring sells a smartphone service that monitors client locations and blood alcohol content for supervision agencies. Clients are monitored with active or passive GPS and blood alcohol content readings taken on a compact portable breathalyzer paired with a smartphone app. An integrated calendar sends reminders for court dates and other events. Violations are sent immediately by text message or email. A monitoring center reviews check-ins from electronic devices at all hours.

The product is aimed at criminal justice agencies. A video conferencing feature lets supervising officers hold virtual meetings and home visits and verify participant locations. Named settings for the service include parole, probation, pretrial, re-entry courts, drug courts, treatment facilities and a private probation company.
Client data for probation and pretrial services is stored with Amazon Web Services. The app replaces older monitoring hardware with a phone the person under supervision already owns.

paragraphs: Tybera Development Group is a Utah-based company that provides electronic filing, case management and document management software for attorneys, courts and government agencies. Alpine is a browser-based case management system that handles cases, parties, events and calendaring across the lifecycle of a case. CEDAR is document archiving and storage technology designed to fit the needs of courts and government agencies. It maintains index information about where documents are stored in relation to the case and for revision control.

The homepage says support is provided to customers, with a link to get product support. News headlines on that page name Cumberland County Courts and Fort Bragg as partners offering a domestic violence eFiling system. before.name: CourtSmart
before.description: Digital courtroom recording and speech recognition systems for courts

paragraphs: CourtSmart designs and installs digital audio and video recording systems for courtrooms. The same recording technology is offered for hearing rooms, interview rooms and conferences.

Audio moves from the courtroom to recording servers or workstations over Dante digital transport. A room can record on its own PC or laptop or onto networked central servers, with automatic archiving either way. Staff can annotate proceedings, and the recording system can be tied into a case management system. A docket display application pulls calendar and public access information from the court's case management system.

The company says its recording systems capture millions of hours of legal proceedings in the United States and internationally. Integration is built on ODBC open standards. For remote hearings, a portable system can be taken along and the recordings uploaded afterwards to a central site for permanent storage.

paragraphs: equivant sells software for the justice process, listed on its home page as court, pretrial, treatment court, admin law, drug testing LIS, supervision, and corrections. The court solution is described as a way to simplify case management and improve access to justice, and the pretrial solution as a way to expedite release decisions, reduce FTAs, and track key data points. Other listed solutions manage drug testing programs and deliver timely results, and optimize classification and custody management for corrections.

The home page lists the organizations served as courts, administrative courts and commissions, tribunals, dispute resolution agencies, corrections, supervision, pretrial, drug testing, and treatment court. A team page says three software companies serving the justice industry together provide products and services for courts, probation and parole agencies, jails and prisons, pretrial agencies, drug and treatment courts, drug testing labs, and public attorneys. The about page reports more than 350+ justice agency customers internationally, supported over a span of four decades.

equivant describes itself as a portfolio of solutions built through both organic development and acquisitions, bringing together technology businesses focused on the justice community. The about page names Constellation Software as the parent company.

before.name: CourtCall
before.description: Remote appearance and virtual hearing services for courts

paragraphs: CourtCall sells a remote appearance service that lets attorneys and other participants take part in court proceedings without traveling to the courthouse. The company says its platform can meet the remote collaboration needs of a court, law firm, administrative agency or corrections facility.

Appearances run over video, audio or telephone. Attorneys use it to appear for routine matters in civil, family, criminal, probate and bankruptcy cases. Participants schedule, continue or cancel an appearance before the hearing. Before doing so, the site asks users to check its list of participating courts.

CourtCall states that it was established in 1995 to make remote court appearances simple, accessible and affordable for all parties. It describes providing supported remote legal collaboration services throughout the United States, Canada and worldwide. A home page announcement says the company was the successful bidder on the Colorado Judicial Department solicitation RFP #25005 and entered into an agreement with the department.

Its GovLink product is aimed at agencies such as child support, insurance and public utilities. Its PeachCourt product handles electronic filing and is described as practically a direct line to the clerk's office.

GovLink combines system integrations, document management, workflow and notifications. The stated payoff is that customers spend more time on their core mission. PeachCourt captures filing information, documents and payments in one pass. It is built to integrate with any case management system. Courts using it are told they will not deal with merchant accounts, bad checks or chargebacks. Family, criminal and appeals cases are among those that can move from paper to online.

GreenCourt Legal Technologies, LLC was founded in 2014. Ownership sits with a small number of individuals. Those same people manage the company day to day, and it calls itself financially stable. Headquarters is in Carrollton, Georgia. Teammates also live in California, New Jersey and many places in between.

before.name: Judicial Systems
before.description: Genesis jury management software for courts

paragraphs: Judicial Systems sells jury management software to courts. Its product Genesis was developed to give courts a way to manage jury operations, and the company says it simplifies juror communications and stabilizes juror ratios.

Services listed on the solutions page include systems training, jury wheel creation, integration work, and printing and mailing of juror summonses. The page describes API-driven integrations between Genesis and existing case management and court systems. That page says the random selection process was tested for 18 months before approval from the U.S. Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals. Homepage copy states that over 180 courts across the country rely on the company to power their court operations. The about page describes four decades of experience and partnerships with 180 courts nationwide. It also describes solutions that streamline processes and improve communication for court administrators and jurors.

before.name: CommunityPass
before.description: Online registration, membership, and payments for parks & rec departments and community schools - exhibited at NRPA 2026, ASBO School Business 2026

paragraphs: CommunityPass is cloud-based software that powers schools, recreation centers, community organizations, and sports leagues. It comes from Capturepoint, whose founder the company names as Joe Oriente.

The product began in 2002 with a town Sports Council overwhelmed by hundreds of paper registration forms as athletic sign-ups climbed. The answer was a single account on one website through which families reach registration for every participating organization in town. Departments can offer registration for classes, activities, programs, and trips, with options to buy merchandise and tickets. Payments accept multiple forms with recurring billing and plans while maintaining PCI compliance.

Check-in and check-out are contactless and digital, with pick-up timestamps and real-time emergency contact information for authorized parents. Staff can choose from 300+ pre-built reports covering attendance, financial, roster, and statistical data, or build their own. The company says CommunityPass has grown to serve parks and recreation organizations and schools all across the country.

paragraphs: Amilia sells software that pulls memberships, program registration, payments, and reporting into one system. The customer it describes is the community organization that runs classes, memberships, and facilities for local families.

Registration happens through a branded online store that can stand on its own or sit inside the organization's existing website. Age or skill restrictions and defined registration periods control who can sign up for which activity. Waitlists fill open spots as soon as a registration is cancelled. On the facilities side, a calendar keeps bookings, activities, and rental contracts in sync so staff can see which space is in use and when. Access rules decide which memberships, activities, or passes open the door at each entry point.

before.name: Daxko
before.description: Membership and operations software for YMCAs, JCCs, and community rec centers - exhibited at AB Show 2026

competitors.why: Both sell membership and program management to YMCA, JCC and community rec center directors
Both sell membership and activity registration to community rec centers and nonprofit program operators
Both sell membership and booking software to community recreation centers

paragraphs: Daxko sells membership management software and built-in payments to health and wellness organizations. Its original and core market is nonprofit community organizations: YMCAs, Boys & Girls Clubs, JCCs and community centers. For them it offers Daxko Operations and Daxko Core, which cover membership, program and child care registration, scheduling, billing, point-of-sale, facility access and fundraising, plus Daxko Engage and Engage Pro for member engagement and retention. Over time it has added a large portfolio for private fitness operators. Club Automation and CSI serve health clubs and multipurpose facilities. Zen Planner and SugarWOD serve boutique studios, CrossFit-style gyms and martial arts schools. Motionsoft, Daxko Exercise and FitnessForce serve multi-location and franchise operators, with FitnessForce built for international markets. Other add-ons include Daxko Payments, GroupEx Pro for class scheduling, Playerspace for league management, Elevate Wellness, revenue recovery services, and newer AI products (a FrontDesk assistant, AI-built websites and member analytics).

Daxko replaces an operator's separate systems for member records, billing, class and program scheduling, check-in and marketing with one system of record. For a YMCA, that means members join, register for programs, book classes and pay online, and the front desk handles check-in, point-of-sale and billing in the same platform. Finance teams get the accounting and fundraising tools nonprofits need. Payments are a large part of the business model: Daxko processes the recurring dues and fees that run through the software, and its revenue recovery service chases failed payments. The company says its software runs in about 19,000 fitness and wellness facilities in 55 countries, serving more than 25 million members. It sells directly, and I found no government contract vehicles. One caveat for your list: Daxko's buyers are nonprofits and private gyms, not government agencies, so it sits next to govtech rather than in it. Its main public-sector overlap is municipal rec centers that run like YMCAs.

Daxko was founded in 1998 and is headquartered at 600 University Park Place in Birmingham, Alabama, with a second hub in Denver. Pamlico Capital backed it earlier and sold to GI Partners in September 2016, when Daxko had about 1,200 customers and 195 employees. In October 2021, Genstar Capital joined GI Partners as a co-investor in a recapitalization meant to fund product development, sales and acquisitions. Much of the current brand lineup came from that acquisition strategy.

paragraphs: Univerus Sport & Recreation is the sport and recreation division of Univerus Software Inc. It sells two cloud products to public-sector and institutional buyers. Univerus Rec is recreation management software for municipal parks and recreation departments, community centres, campus recreation at universities and colleges, camps and nonprofits. It covers facility booking across multiple locations, online program registration (custom pricing, discounts, waitlists, attendance, digital waivers), membership management (family accounts, recurring payments, a self-service member portal), point-of-sale with multiple registers and inventory, and staff scheduling with shift trading and certification tracking. Univerus Sport is aimed at university and college athletic departments, school district sports programs and leagues. It handles athlete registration, athlete and coach records, eligibility and compliance tracking, email and SMS messaging, team travel, wellness checks and historical awards. Both products run on a shared "UNITY" platform with single sign-on.

The pitch is that one system replaces paper forms, spreadsheets and older recreation systems. In Univerus Rec, a resident books a gym or field, signs up for a class or buys a family membership through the online portal or on mobile. Payment goes through Univerus's own payment processing. Staff then run the front desk from the same system, with scheduling, reporting and financials all in one place. It also connects to TeamLinkt, a league-management tool, and has an API. On the athletics side, Univerus Sport takes eligibility and compliance paperwork out of spreadsheets and email and tracks it against a central athlete record. The division says it has more than 500 sport and recreation clients, including about 325 municipalities and 100+ universities and organizations, and manages over 83,000 athletes. Its customers are mostly in Canada, with a growing U.S. base; recent wins include the Township of Champlain and Carleton's Dominion-Chalmers Centre.

paragraphs: Esri builds ArcGIS, its geographic information system software for mapping and spatial analysis. The company describes itself as the global market leader in GIS software, location intelligence, and mapping. Its stated audience is business, government, and society.

ArcGIS is presented as enterprise technology that integrates and connects data through the context of geography. The premise is that hidden patterns, trends, and relationships emerge once data is visualized and analyzed on a map. Beyond maps and analysis, the company says its technology speeds data sharing and collaboration. For agencies that want to keep everything in house, there is a self-hosted edition for mapping, analytics, and data management.

Esri says it has supported customers with geographic science and geospatial analytics since 1969. Officials working in public safety, transportation, infrastructure, health and human services, and other fields use the technology to support high-level decisions. At the local level, the company says community leaders apply it to economic development, public works, and urban planning. Published stories include the US Census Bureau modernizing its entire census process with GIS.

paragraphs: EagleView sells aerial imagery and property data drawn from an archive the company puts at more than 3.5 billion high-resolution images. Public agencies are one audience, with the imagery aimed at tax assessment, zoning enforcement, emergency response and infrastructure planning.

The subscription imagery product refreshes annually at 2-inch resolution, with an option to upgrade. The company says its 1-inch imagery carries nine times more detail than 3-inch imagery. Captures include straight-down orthogonal views for mapping and measurement and angled oblique views of building sides. A separate archive holds more than 25 years of imagery covering 96 percent of the United States population. New content is added daily, with annual refreshes across metro areas and high-growth regions. Customers view imagery in a browser tool or pull it through API connections into GIS, CAD, CAMA or analytics systems.
The site states that 20 of the top 20 insurers rely on the company. Governments, insurers, utilities, AEC firms and environmental professionals are named as users of the imagery archive.

paragraphs: Cyclomedia sells geospatial data built from street-level imagery, lidar point clouds, and aerial data covering public space. Public authorities are a core market, using it to manage streets, buildings, and public assets. Utility and energy providers use it to plan, inspect, and manage their networks.

Street Smart, the company's viewer, brings 360 degree imagery, lidar, and map layers into one browser-based workspace. From the desk, users measure distances along facades, pavements, and openings. Automated analysis detects pavement defects, surface types, and deterioration in high-resolution imagery. Property valuation is another stated use, supported by current visual evidence and measurements. Open integrations and APIs connect the data to existing GIS and asset management systems.

The company says it has worked in geospatial capture and visualisation for more than 40 years with public authorities across Europe and beyond. Specialised capture vehicles survey cities and regions throughout the year. Routes are coordinated with local authorities to limit disruption. Its case studies page lists a digital twin created for the London Borough of Harrow from street imagery and lidar.

quote.text: Shift more work from the field to the office by using Street Smart and work more efficiently.

before.name: EagleView
before.description: Aerial imagery and property data analytics for county assessors, GIS, and insurers - exhibited at IAAO 2026, URISA GIS-Pro 2026

paragraphs: EagleView sells aerial imagery and property data drawn from an archive the company puts at more than 3.5 billion high-resolution images. Public agencies are one audience, with the imagery aimed at tax assessment, zoning enforcement, emergency response and infrastructure planning.

The subscription imagery product refreshes annually at 2-inch resolution, with an option to upgrade. The company says its 1-inch imagery carries nine times more detail than 3-inch imagery. Captures include straight-down orthogonal views for mapping and measurement and angled oblique views of building sides. A separate archive holds more than 25 years of imagery covering 96 percent of the United States population. New content is added daily, with annual refreshes across metro areas and high-growth regions. Customers view imagery in a browser tool or pull it through API connections into GIS, CAD, CAMA or analytics systems.
The site states that 20 of the top 20 insurers rely on the company. Governments, insurers, utilities, AEC firms and environmental professionals are named as users of the imagery archive.

paragraphs: DATAMARK Technologies sells geospatial data services and location software for public safety, spanning the whole GIS life cycle from data creation through updates and maintenance. The company took its current shape when DATAMARK and DDTI combined, a union its chief executive calls a significant milestone for both.

On the services side, project managers and analysts prepare GIS data for NG9-1-1 or raise its accuracy for call routing. One named service is the Address Comparison Evaluation, shortened to ACE. The company states that its Location Information Server is the only NENA i3 standards-compliant option, supporting carriers through Phase 1 and Phase 2 deployments. A separate product called INSIDE applies indoor geospatial data so public safety, facility and school stakeholders can keep remote oversight of a campus.

The staff are described as former 9-1-1 directors, public safety subject matter experts and GIS professionals. The site points to work with the state of Idaho on its journey to GIS data readiness. It also cites an indoor mapping partnership with Allegany County, Maryland. An announcement on the page notes that Michael Baker International was selected by the U.S. Army to develop NG9-1-1 GIS and addressing data at 54 Army installations.

before.name: Regrid
before.description: Nationwide parcel data and property mapping licensed to government agencies

paragraphs: Regrid sells standardized parcel data covering North America and Europe under a single schema. Those parcel boundaries carry ownership details, zoning rules, building footprints, and demographics in one view. Coverage runs to every county in the United States. Canadian parcels and European parcel data across 20 countries extend the same land data beyond one market.

Delivery options include enterprise file delivery, an API with tiles and an MCP server, and self-serve county and state downloads from the data store. A hosted Feature Service connects the parcel layers into ArcGIS Pro and ArcGIS Online. A property app for desktop and mobile handles parcel lookup, fieldwork, saved places, notes, and parcel tracking.

Regrid states that the parcel layer supports enterprise teams across real estate, infrastructure, government, energy, conservation, research, and technology. Government use described on the same page covers planning, public services, community development, transparency, research, and land-related decision-making. The customers page describes the audience as enterprise teams that depend on parcel data across jurisdictions.

quote.text: Regrid makes parcel data easier to access, understand, and use, so people can make better decisions about land across communities, markets, and borders.

provenance.quote: Standardized parcel data across North America and Europe
Precise parcel boundaries enriched with ownership details, zoning rules, building footprints, and demographics in one unified view.

Scale across borders with standardized European parcel data across 20 countries and counting, built for teams that need reliable land data beyond one market.
Whether you need a national enterprise dataset, a developer-ready API, a self-serve download, an Esri-compatible service, or an AI-ready MCP connection, Regrid meets your workflow where it is.
Connect to hosted parcel data through a secure Feature Service URL and work with Regrid layers in ArcGIS Pro, ArcGIS Online, and supported Esri applications, without maintaining large static files.
For fast parcel lookup, fieldwork, property research, saved places, notes, and parcel tracking.

Today, that foundation supports enterprise teams across real estate, infrastructure, government, energy, conservation, research, and technology, along with millions of Regrid app users and the wider public.
