paragraphs: Motorola Solutions builds and connects technologies to protect people, property and places, supporting the collaboration between public safety agencies and enterprises. Its public safety lineup includes APX portable and mobile radios and ASTRO radio systems. On the command center side it sells NG911 call routing and call handling and Computer-Aided Dispatch. The company also designs video security and access control systems.

For police users the APX NEXT smart radio comes in single-band and multi-band configurations. The APX 8500 all-band mobile radio adds interoperability, Wi-Fi connectivity and Bluetooth in the vehicle. Vehicle routers keep first responders connected to broadband so they can reach real-time intelligence on the road. Its broadband products can run on FirstNET or on commercial carrier LTE networks. Managed, support and professional services are sold alongside to keep those systems secure and current.

Customer stories on the site include the Ouachita Parish Sheriff's Office, Peel Police, Nampa PD and York Regional Police, which serves 1.2 million residents. Hutto Independent School District uses the VB400 body camera to capture evidence in its schools. The home page announces the completed acquisition of D-Fend Solutions, which the company describes as a counter-drone technology firm.

The APX 8500 all-band mobile radio combines unlimited interoperability, secure Wi-Fi connectivity, integrated Bluetooth and purpose-built design.
Vehicle routers keep first responders connected to broadband so they can access real-time intelligence on the road.
Our broadband solutions can operate on FirstNET or commercial carrier LTE networks.
We provide managed, support and professional services to keep your solutions secure, optimized and current.
Threat monitoring and expert guidance help to protect York Regional Police’s mission-critical network, enhancing safety for the 1.2 million residents they serve.
Hutto Independent School District (ISD) relies on the VB400 body camera every day to capture evidence and foster trust in the school community.
An industry leader in counter-drone technology

paragraphs: FLASHNET sells inteliLIGHT, a remote management system for street lighting made up of lamp controllers and software. The customers it names are city managers, street lighting operators and lamp manufacturers around the world.

Controllers are built for both individual lamp and lighting segment control. City examples on the home page run over NB-IoT and cellular communications. The company page puts energy savings at up to 35 percent through smart dimming scheduling, with overall operational costs down by up to 42 percent. The system is presented as compatible with major smart city standards.

FLASHNET is a technology company based in Brasov, Romania, that combines hardware and software into services for cities. It says that since 2005 more than 400 million people have seen the benefits of inteliLIGHT, in hundreds of cities on six continents. The company has been part of Lucy Group since 2022.

paragraphs: Planet sells Earth observation data products drawn from its own satellite constellations. Planet Monitoring supplies near daily coverage at 3.7 meter resolution in four multispectral bands, RGB and Near Infrared. Satellite Tasking adds site specific SkySat high resolution imagery, and Planetary Variables quantifies attributes like soil moisture, biomass, and land surface temperature.

Access runs on a subscription model, with images ordered through Planet's APIs, web application, and GIS integrations. The archive of high resolution images dates from 2009. Planet reports over 300 million square kilometers of imagery collected each day. The monitoring page describes the New Mexico State Land Office using Planet Monitoring to uncover 53 trespasses which yielded $2.7 million in back payments. Bayer and Pan Pac are named on the same page, Bayer for Planet Monitoring and Pan Pac for PlanetScope imagery.

before.name: LineVision
before.description: Non-contact transmission line monitoring and dynamic line ratings for utilities

paragraphs: LineVision sells an integrated intelligence platform that delivers Dynamic Line Ratings and Situational Awareness for transmission networks. Dynamic Line Ratings covers real-time and forecasted transmission capacity at every span across networks. Forecasted ratings extend hourly up to 240 hours, or 10 days. Items listed under Dynamic Line Ratings include FERC 881 and NERC FAC-008 compliance.

Situational Awareness provides real-time monitoring of physical risks and environmental conditions on critical transmission lines. That monitoring runs on RS-1 sensors that gather continuous, hyperlocal data around critical transmission rights-of-way. Detection and alerting cover conductor hazards including galloping, clashing, asynchronous motion, and unusual sag. Other alerts listed cover conductor icing, fallen trees, and unauthorized people or equipment in the ROW.

LineVision states that it works with 7 to the 10 largest utilities in the US. Named customers on these pages include National Grid, Xcel Energy, Avangrid, and New York Transco. Service capabilities listed include 24/7 customer support for operational DLR and EMS integration described as NERC-CIP compliant. The home page states that LineVision solutions are US-domiciled and NERC-CIP approved, with the SMS certified to ISO 27001:2022.

paragraphs: Epoch Solutions Group sells software to utilities that want to modernize how field work gets done. Its main platform, EpochField, is built for electric, gas, water, and telecom providers and gives field crews tools to inspect, maintain, and respond.

before.name: AiDash
before.description: Satellite + AI vegetation management (IVMS) and climate/asset risk SaaS for utilities

paragraphs: AiDASH sells software that electric utilities use to find vegetation, asset, wildfire and storm risk before it takes the grid down. The method starts with continuous satellite monitoring, then adds targeted aerial, vehicle-mounted and on-demand inspection.

Very high resolution satellite passes refresh vegetation health data up to twelve times a year. Higher-cadence imagery tracks fuel load, moisture and burnability up to seven times a week. One system covers asset inspection and monitoring. Another handles wildfire situational awareness and risk mitigation. A storm system predicts outages 120 hours ahead so crews can be pre-positioned. The platform exposes REST APIs for automation or for integrating with systems a utility already runs.

The company says it was founded by serial entrepreneurs in 2019. Its about page claims more than 150 customers of every size around the world. The platform page states SOC 2 Type 2 certification. A news item on the site announces that Schneider Electric agreed to acquire AiDASH for $350 million.

after.name: AiDash
after.description: Satellite + AI vegetation management (IVMS) and climate/asset risk SaaS for utilities - exhibited at DISTRIBUTECH 2026

paragraphs: AiDASH sells software that electric utilities use to find vegetation, asset, wildfire and storm risk before it takes the grid down. The method starts with continuous satellite monitoring, then adds targeted aerial, vehicle-mounted and on-demand inspection.

Very high resolution satellite passes refresh vegetation health data up to twelve times a year. Higher-cadence imagery tracks fuel load, moisture and burnability up to seven times a week. One system covers asset inspection and monitoring. Another handles wildfire situational awareness and risk mitigation. A storm system predicts outages 120 hours ahead so crews can be pre-positioned. The platform exposes REST APIs for automation or for integrating with systems a utility already runs.

The company says it was founded by serial entrepreneurs in 2019. Its about page claims more than 150 customers of every size around the world. The platform page states SOC 2 Type 2 certification. A news item on the site announces that Schneider Electric agreed to acquire AiDASH for $350 million.

paragraphs: Esri builds ArcGIS, its geographic information system software for mapping and spatial analysis. The company describes itself as the global market leader in GIS software, location intelligence, and mapping. Its stated audience is business, government, and society.

ArcGIS is presented as enterprise technology that integrates and connects data through the context of geography. The premise is that hidden patterns, trends, and relationships emerge once data is visualized and analyzed on a map. Beyond maps and analysis, the company says its technology speeds data sharing and collaboration. For agencies that want to keep everything in house, there is a self-hosted edition for mapping, analytics, and data management.

Esri says it has supported customers with geographic science and geospatial analytics since 1969. Officials working in public safety, transportation, infrastructure, health and human services, and other fields use the technology to support high-level decisions. At the local level, the company says community leaders apply it to economic development, public works, and urban planning. Published stories include the US Census Bureau modernizing its entire census process with GIS.

before.name: Virtual Peaker
before.description: Cloud DERMS and demand flexibility software for municipal utilities and co-ops

paragraphs: Virtual Peaker sells cloud software that lets an electric utility reach the smart devices already sitting in homes and businesses and use them to shave peak load and cost. The buyers are utilities standing up demand response programs.

Three suites make up the product, and the company presents them together as a virtual power plant platform that aggregates distributed energy resources at the edge of the grid. The Shift suite is the dispatch side, aggregating resources at homes and at commercial and industrial sites to hold down peak market costs and defer new construction. The Relay suite handles the customer side, signing people up and paying out the incentives. A utility can run several program types at once across electric vehicles, thermostats, water heaters and batteries.

The company describes partnerships with more than thirty device types, from thermostats to electric vehicle chargers. It states that the platform is SOC 2 Type 2 certified. Municipal energy providers are named as one audience, using demand response to meet grid goals and engage customers. One published case study covers Sacramento Municipal Utility District optimizing hot water heater efficiency on the platform.

before.name: Daupler
before.description: After-hours call intake, incident triage and crew dispatch software for water, sewer and electric utilities and public works departments - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026

paragraphs: Daupler sells a response management system that gives teams the information and tools to respond to service requests and emergencies. Public works, utilities, and service organizations of all sizes are named as the users. The work runs from odor complaints to water main breaks.

The company runs call centers that take intake calls, notify staff about urgent issues, and document noncritical calls for the next day. An automated roster callout feature forms crews without anyone working a phone list by hand. Event detection spots incidents affecting multiple people and stops repeat calls from being dispatched. For outbound messages, the system sends a text or a recorded voice message depending on whether the number is mobile or a landline. The platform sits at the center of existing information systems and combines their data into one view of an incident. Site arrival times and crew check-ins are logged to help make sure crews get back safely.
The company states clients are seeing a 20-75% reduction in callouts. Its pages describe the City of Durham integrating the system with CityWorks.

before.name: Heimdall Power
before.description: Dynamic line rating sensors (Neuron) for transmission utilities

paragraphs: Heimdall Power sells sensors and software to electric utilities, with capacity tools meant to help them safely adjust transmission limits, improve operational planning and stay compliant with industry standards. The company was founded in Norway in 2016.

Its dynamic line rating offering combines physical and virtual Neurons to take real-time, on-line measurements. The sensors report temperature, current and inclination on the conductor. Deployment is handled by an autonomous drone installation system that the company says places Neurons in remote or hard-to-reach areas. A facility ratings module consolidates all ratings into one unified system and is aimed at simplifying NERC FAC-008 compliance. Further tools give grid operators real-time visibility into threats like icing, line movement, electrical faults and wildfire risks.

The about page states that the company has grown 10x in two years, raised a $25M Series B and expanded with a North American headquarters in Charlotte, NC. A news item on the site reports that Heimdall Power was selected by Statnett for a new Dynamic Line Rating project.

before.name: Cyclomedia
before.description: Vehicle-captured 360 street imagery and lidar with AI analytics for local governments and utilities - exhibited at URISA GIS-Pro 2026

roles.title: Key Account Executive - Central Government, Infrastructure & Public Safety - Belgium

paragraphs: Cyclomedia sells geospatial data built from street-level imagery, lidar point clouds, and aerial data covering public space. Public authorities are a core market, using it to manage streets, buildings, and public assets. Utility and energy providers use it to plan, inspect, and manage their networks.

before.description: LED roadway and area light retrofits for utilities and municipalities

paragraphs: Evluma makes LED lighting for streets, roadways and outdoor areas. Its area light is pitched at utilities as the standard fixture for that job.

The roadway range is sold by wattage, starting with a 30 to 100 watt streetlight. The largest of them reaches 300 watts. For decorative fixtures the company argues that the point is the right light, not the brightest light. Not every job means a new fixture, since some are solved by retrofitting existing luminaires. Wireless control aimed at cutting maintenance is part of the same catalog.

Evluma traces its perspective on lighting to a background in LED photo-finishing equipment. It says many of its products are patented. The company also runs a supplier diversity program that seeks out small, local, minority, disadvantaged, women-owned, HUBZone and veteran-owned businesses as suppliers. Federal definitions are used for those categories.

before.name: CyberLock, Inc.
before.description: Electronic key-centric access control: programmable CyberKey smart keys, retrofit electronic lock cylinders and CyberAudit management software for auditing and scheduling access to gates, cabinets and remote assets. - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026, ITS America 2026

paragraphs: CyberLock, Inc. sells a key-centric electronic access control system meant to increase security, accountability and key control across an organization. Its electronic cylinders retrofit into existing door hardware without power or wiring.

Because the wire between the lock and the managing software is eliminated, locks can be installed almost anywhere. The company describes the result as the convenience of a mechanical key system plus the access permission and tracking of an electronic one. Key control cabinets automatically program and dispense the smart keys. A patented FlashLock option provides keyless access control from a smartphone, tablet or iPad.

Stated uses include airports, where the system can secure hangars, perimeter and interior gates, baggage and restricted areas. Water and power utilities are another, covering substations, reservoirs, equipment and storage areas. Corporate uses listed run to classrooms, computer carts and employee and student files. The news section reports that the CyberKey Blue 4 and Dynamic Audit Events both received Security Today's 2026 Government Security Awards.

before.name: EnergyHub
before.description: DERMS and virtual power plant programs for utilities including public power

paragraphs: EnergyHub sells utilities software for building virtual power plants, helping them scale VPPs to manage load growth and renewables. The resources involved are customer-side devices such as connected thermostats, solar and storage systems, and electric vehicles.

A single platform holds all of a utility's distributed energy resources. Control runs year-round and across resource types, based on price signals and customer rates. The stated aims are to relieve congestion, protect assets, and defer infrastructure investments. The company also points to a deep partner ecosystem behind the platform.

EnergyHub says it has been delivering load control programs since 2009. One customer story describes work with National Grid on a pay-for-performance residential battery program in Massachusetts. Another describes a thermostat demand response program with Ontario's Independent Electricity System Operator to reduce peak summer load. That program enrolled more than 100,000 homes within six months. EnergyHub is an independent subsidiary of Alarm.com, listed on Nasdaq as ALRM. A newsroom item reports its acquisition of Resideo Grid Services.

paragraphs: Activu makes software for control rooms and command centers, the places where operators watch incidents unfold together in real time. The company describes its product as a network-based visual intelligence software solution for mission-critical operations. It also designs, builds, and supports the rooms themselves, including security operations centers, fusion centers, and video walls.

The platform, called vis/ability, serves real time crime centers, emergency operations centers, and other security operations centers. One listed addition is active shooter recognition. A separate version is presented as a software platform for federal and military command centers. The platform is certified in the ServiceNow Store, where a critical incident can pull the relevant applications and information into a dashboard for IT and executive stakeholders.

The about page organizes customers by sector, beginning with traffic management centers and departments of transportation. Rail and mass transit operators are listed next to airports and federal air travel agencies. Utility operations appear as well, including electricity generation and transmission. Public safety users are named too, covering emergency operations centers and fire, police, and disaster response. Federal buyers listed include the Department of Homeland Security.

before.name: Tantalus Systems
before.description: Smart grid AMI and grid analytics for public power utilities and co-ops - exhibited at APPA Public Power 2026

paragraphs: Tantalus is a technology company selling grid modernization systems to public power and electric cooperative utilities. It has been delivering data-centric products to that market for more than 35 years.

The products sit on the Tantalus Grid Modernization Platform, a modular architecture meant to move data across devices, systems and vendors. One piece is edge-computing metering infrastructure aimed at resiliency, reliability and lower total cost of ownership. Another handles load management and distributed energy resources sitting behind the meter. A gateway device fits any ANSI meter socket and adds visibility and control behind the meter without replacing the meter itself.

Utilities across North America partner with the company on distribution grid work, with published case studies including one in Bolivar, Tennessee. Tantalus Systems trades on the TSX under the symbol GRID and on OTCQX. It is based in Burnaby, British Columbia. Recent announcements include a debt restructuring and an annual survey of how utilities view grid modernization.

paragraphs: Boston Dynamics builds mobile robots that companies use to automate tedious and hazardous work in manufacturing, logistics and other industries. Its product line covers Spot, Stretch, Atlas and Orbit. Spot is a mobile robot that automates sensing and inspection and captures data wherever it is sent. The company states that over 1,500 Spot robots are in customer hands today.

Spot works on factory floors, construction sites and research labs. As a sensing platform it gives teams insight into routine operations, site health or potentially hazardous situations. In energy and natural resources it performs inspections in energized, radioactive or otherwise hazardous areas. Operators can also use it to remotely investigate, assess and de-escalate tense or hazardous situations, reducing the risk to personnel. With the Spot Arm, operators can handle tasks such as nuclear material handling or suspicious package investigation from a safe distance. Standard payload configurations cover inspection, public safety and innovation, including a Government & Public Safety Kit.

Stretch, the company's warehouse robot, handles cases and unloads trailers. Orbit, its fleet management software, manages autonomous tasks, operates robots remotely and analyzes data within the context of a facility map. Atlas, a humanoid robot, is in early field testing with Hyundai on real-world sequencing tasks. The company has announced a new 323,000 square foot facility in Waltham, Massachusetts.

paragraphs: KloudGin sells work and asset management software to water and wastewater utilities. Gas utilities are a second market for the same platform. Municipalities and other public sector agencies are a third.

One part of the platform handles construction work management for complex projects, built on utility industry expertise. An enterprise asset management side unifies assets and workforce to optimize operations. Work management gives crews a view of assets, work orders, records and AI-native decision support. Prebuilt modules cover specific utility jobs such as automating fire hydrant maintenance. Others handle 811 ticket automation for dig requests. Another helps crews identify, document and replace lead service lines. GIS capabilities are embedded to support location-based customer service, and a separate adapter serves SAP customers.

An IDC MarketScape evaluation cited on the site names the company a Leader in utilities enterprise asset management. The company has announced a partnership with Black & Veatch. Its chief executive is named on the site as Vikram Takru. It also positions itself as a platform choice for cities.

paragraphs: Overstory sells vegetation intelligence to electric utilities, from investor-owned utilities to municipalities and cooperatives. The analysis rests on satellite imagery, which in one European project was used to identify 37 species of vegetation.

The company notes that vegetation management is typically a utility's greatest operations budget item. Its pitch is spending less on unnecessary trimming and more on riskier areas. Utilities can see strike trees, declining trees and hazard trees individually or aggregated. Encroachment risk, hazard trees and species identification can be laid over wildfire risk maps to show where trimming matters most. The same data lets a utility verify and document risk reduction from work that contractors completed.

Risk reports are meant to support data-driven conversations with regulators, insurers and executives. Indra den Bakker and Anniek Schouten founded the company in Lisbon in 2018. The company says it has worked with more than 50 investor-owned utilities and cooperatives across the Americas and Europe.

paragraphs: Skydio makes autonomous drones, along with the docks and software to run them, and sells drone programs to customers from energy networks to neighborhood precincts to battlefields. Those programs cover Drone as First Responder, automated inspection and site security. Dock for X10 positions Skydio X10 drones at a site so that missions launch remotely without anyone present. The smaller Skydio R10 puts eyes indoors before officers enter.

Skydio states that more than 1,500 public safety agencies use its drones. In a Drone as First Responder program, Skydio says its drones launch in under 20 seconds and reach incidents autonomously in under 90 seconds. DFR Command is the software from which remote operators launch and manage drones, respond to multiple calls and stream live video to patrol and command. It integrates with RapidSOS and CAD at dispatch, Axon Fusus for live operations, and automatic evidence upload into Axon Evidence. Skydio's customer stories include Brookhaven PD, which it says reached 30 second response times after deploying 8 Docks.

Skydio Site Security uses the same dock-based drones to verify alarms, patrol perimeters and deliver live visibility across a site. Video streams into Genetec or Milestone, and flights launch automatically when triggered by alarms or access control events. Skydio says its data is encrypted in transit and at rest and that it aligns to SOC 2, ISO 27001 and NIST frameworks.

paragraphs: Fulcrum sells a field operations platform that organizations use to run, record and close out work done away from an office. The pitch is aimed at teams still working from paper forms and a scatter of separate point tools.

Crews are given location-enabled apps on ordinary mobile devices in place of paperwork. They capture points, lines and polygons using the device's own GPS or a Bluetooth receiver. The collected records move into ArcGIS or other systems through APIs and formats such as shapefiles and GeoJSON. The company treats working without a signal as a baseline rather than an add-on.

State and local government is one of the named audiences, alongside utilities, construction and public works, with inspections and documentation for community projects. The home page states nearly 3,000 companies and 50,000 users in over 100 countries. On security, the company points to SCIM and SOC 2 compliance, and its timeline records an independent SOC 2 Type 1 certification. Spatial Networks Inc. is named as the maker of Fulcrum, and the company reports acquiring Wildnote to deepen environmental compliance work.

paragraphs: Motorola Solutions builds and connects technologies to protect people, property and places, supporting the collaboration between public safety agencies and enterprises. Its public safety lineup includes APX portable and mobile radios and ASTRO radio systems. On the command center side it sells NG911 call routing and call handling and Computer-Aided Dispatch. The company also designs video security and access control systems.

For police users the APX NEXT smart radio comes in single-band and multi-band configurations. The APX 8500 all-band mobile radio adds interoperability, Wi-Fi connectivity and Bluetooth in the vehicle. Vehicle routers keep first responders connected to broadband so they can reach real-time intelligence on the road. Its broadband products can run on FirstNET or on commercial carrier LTE networks. Managed, support and professional services are sold alongside to keep those systems secure and current.

Customer stories on the site include the Ouachita Parish Sheriff's Office, Peel Police, Nampa PD and York Regional Police, which serves 1.2 million residents. Hutto Independent School District uses the VB400 body camera to capture evidence in its schools. The home page announces the completed acquisition of D-Fend Solutions, which the company describes as a counter-drone technology firm.

paragraphs: GridUnity sells software for transmission and distribution interconnection, aimed at making energy project approvals faster. It is built for the parties on both sides of an interconnection request, including ISOs, RTOs, utilities, developers and transmission owners.

The platform runs the life cycle from application intake to commissioning in one place. It is delivered as configurable software as a service, which the company says lets customers meet federal and state orders as those evolve. Near real-time data sharing among developers, utilities and regulators is offered as a way to cut disputes and speed studies. The company states compliance with NIST 800-171 and SOC 2 Type II standards.

Products are broken out for transmission, for large load and for distribution. On its own record the company cites a five-year research and development strategy focused on AI, automation and predictive analytics. It also cites $45 million in matching Department of Energy funding and GRIP award recognition. Collaboration with research institutions and government agencies is described as part of that work.

paragraphs: IQGeo gives telecom and utility operators a single platform to plan, design, build, and operate their physical network infrastructure. It is aimed at telecom, fiber, and utility network operators, including planners, engineers, and construction teams.

Network Manager Telecom is built to plan, build, and operate fiber and coax networks with accurate data, simple field tools, and automated AI quality checks. Field staff can download their work area, update records offline, and sync changes back automatically. Construction photos are audited with real-time visual AI to verify quality, completeness, and compliance at scale. A companion product, Network Manager Electric, is described as built for geospatial work execution, combining geospatial intelligence with AI-powered workflows across the full lifecycle.

Buyers choose between two deployment options, an IQGeo SaaS deployment or a private cloud deployment they host themselves. The hosted option is listed with ISO/IEC 27001:2013 certification. The private cloud option is pitched at operators needing bespoke integration with legacy GIS and OSS/BSS systems. The company says electric and gas utilities rely on it for asset management, grid modernization, inspection and field operations. On the telecom side it describes its customers as reaching some of the largest and fastest-growing global telecom operators, managing highly complex, rapidly scaling networks.

paragraphs: SmartWorks sells SmartWorks Compass, a platform that helps electric, water, and gas utilities improve data accuracy, automate operational workflows, and uncover insight through analytics and AI. The platform covers data management, operational intelligence, analytics, automation, and AI capabilities, and its modular structure lets a utility begin with one priority and add capabilities as requirements change. Compass is built to sit alongside systems a utility already runs, and SmartWorks integrates with CIS, AMI, AMR, customer engagement, and other utility environments.

SmartWorks Athena is the AI line, letting utility staff explore operational information in everyday language rather than through custom reports or technical queries. Athena reaches meter-to-cash, AMI, CIS, and operational data through plain-English questions, and it can also support compatible CIS and MDM environments outside SmartWorks Compass.

SmartWorks Connect is a separate portal line that utilities use to give residential and commercial customers self-service access, usage insights, billing details, alerts, and service tools. These pages name electric, water, gas, and multi-commodity utilities as the customers for all of it, and place that work across North America and the Caribbean. The company describes itself as part of Harris Utilities, working alongside established CIS, customer engagement, and complementary utility technology providers.

before.name: Neara
before.description: Physics-based digital twin modeling of grid networks for utilities

paragraphs: Neara sells physics-based digital twin software to electric utilities, which use it to model their networks. The pitch is to unify assets, surroundings and workflows in a single physics-accurate view.

The model is built from a utility's existing LiDAR, imagery, GIS and asset records. Teams then simulate wind, ice, thermal, flood, vegetation, reconductoring and new builds on the real network geometry. Outputs include prioritized hardening plans, regulator-ready reports and field-ready work orders. Solution areas cover resiliency and reliability, wildfire mitigation, asset management, risk and value optimization, and design and construction.

On the asset side, replacement candidates are ranked by measured load rather than by install date. Wildfire work pulls pole loading, asset condition, vegetation, GIS accuracy, weather and consequence into one physics-backed model. Resiliency work prioritizes mitigation by how asset condition, vegetation proximity and environmental conditions interact across the network. Case study quotes on the site are attributed to the chief executive of Essential Energy. Another comes from a general manager of network management at SA Power Networks.

That feed is tens of thousands of global AWS engineering/PM/ops roles, of which SLED account executive roles are a tiny fraction. Any homepage- or careers-page-level scrape of this record will flood SLED JOBS with irrelevant listings - the same practical damage the parent-domain rule exists to prevent, arriving by a different route. paragraphs: Bidgely builds energy analytics software for electric utilities, working from the data their smart meters already collect. The core claim is that a utility can identify what is running inside every home and business from meter data alone, with no surveys or smart plugs.

The platform, called UtilityAI, breaks that meter signal down to appliance level for every customer, grid asset and hour of the year. Utilities use it on the customer side to resolve high bill questions before people call in. On the grid side it is pitched for capacity planning that accounts for distributed energy resources. Program teams are offered targeting for EV and electrification enrollment. There is also a module for discovering and remedying energy theft. The company offers the software as SaaS or deployed inside a utility's own cloud.

Buyers span the utility enterprise, covering customer experience, grid operations and efficiency and electrification programs. Case studies on the site report results such as 238% of contracted savings in the first year of a deployment. Bidgely also runs an annual conference, registration for which is advertised on the home page.

paragraphs: Camus Energy sells software that electric utilities use to interconnect data centers and local generation. What it sells is the flexible grid connection, in which the utility guarantees firm capacity for most of a site's demand and applies conditional limits to the rest.

Camus uses real utility data to map how much additional load each conductor and substation can safely serve in every hour of the year. Utilities then decide what portion of the load is served firmly and set operating limits for the conditional portion. Day-ahead operating forecasts show when those conditional limits will apply, alongside closed loop controls. The platform pulls SCADA data, GIS assets, network models, AMI, and DER telemetry into one consistent system model. Two applications sit on it: FlexConnect for interconnections and ODMS, which gives utilities a unified view of the distribution grid.

The company says it supports investor-owned and public power utilities. It counts 12 or more utility partners across the United States. It states that joint studies with Google, AES, and Princeton's ZERO Lab set the benchmark for how utilities and developers evaluate flexibility and grid capacity. On security, it says OAuth authentication, MFA, role-based access, audit logging, and continuous monitoring protect the platform.

paragraphs: LiveView Technologies, known as LVT, sells rapidly deployable security units configured as mobile trailers, wall mounts, or pole mounts. The company says the units are used by DOTs, oil and gas operators, law enforcement, retailers, construction firms, and housing operators. Each mobile unit runs on its own, carrying solar panels, cellular and available satellite connectivity, lighting, a loud speaker, and a configurable selection of cameras. Pole-mounted versions instead take grid power for fixed coverage where infrastructure already exists.

The software side is a cloud platform reached from a phone or desktop, with a forensic search that sorts footage by keywords such as white car or crowd formation. From a mobile device an operator can zoom in, turn on the lights, and start speaker talk downs. A companion app called SafeNow lets employees set off floodlights, strobes, and audio warnings with one swipe.

On the public side, LVT lists remote monitoring of borders, government buildings, parks, school campuses, healthcare facilities, and military sites. The Arcadia Police Department added LVT Units to its operations for surveillance and crime prevention. Prologis put more than 70 LVT Units across industrial real estate properties in multiple states. LVT has been headquartered in Utah since 2005.

paragraphs: Aurigo Software sells capital program management software to government agencies that plan, build and maintain public infrastructure. It also serves facility owners in areas such as data centers, life sciences, manufacturing, and energy and utilities. The company's platform, Masterworks, brings planning, execution, financials, right of way and analytics together in one system.

On the delivery side it coordinates contracts, schedules, costs and field work so teams can hold to the original plan and keep a complete audit trail. Compliance, funding transparency and governance are meant to sit inside everyday work so public money stays accountable. Agencies can change forms, workflows, business rules and dashboards through configuration rather than code. An AI layer called Lumina supports decision-making with compliance and governance built in, and the company says every insight and recommendation it produces can be audited and traced.

Cities, counties, transit agencies and transportation departments across North America use the platform to manage capital programs, replace legacy systems and automate federal reimbursements. The company claims more than 300 customers and over 20 years of capital program expertise behind the product. It also says the software monitors project signals to catch cost, schedule and delivery risks before they turn critical.

before.name: Technosylva
before.description: Wildfire spread modeling and risk analytics used by CAL FIRE and major utilities

paragraphs: Technosylva sells wildfire and extreme weather risk software to electric utilities and fire agencies. The point of it is turning complicated weather data into something a planning or response team can act on.

For planning, the company combines large numbers of validated fire simulations with historical weather and a customer's own asset data. Its models estimate what an ignition would mean in acres burned, buildings destroyed and people affected. For operations, simulations run nightly to produce the wildfire risk metrics crews plan around. Utilities use the output to target power shutoffs instead of cutting service broadly. Feeds from computer-aided dispatch and IRWIN bring in incidents from federal and state agencies. Flooding, high wind, extreme temperature and winter storms sit in the same view as fire.
The homepage points readers toward Xcel Energy, CAL FIRE and CORE. Bryan Spear is named as chief executive. The company has also announced modeling of urban conflagration in the built environment.

before.name: Anterix
before.description: 900 MHz private LTE spectrum and networks for utilities and public power

paragraphs: Anterix provides private 900 MHz spectrum to utilities so they can run their own wireless networks instead of leaning on commercial carriers. The company frames that as operational control, with the utility owning the communications infrastructure behind essential services. Licensed spectrum is sold together with deployment solutions and ecosystem partners so utilities can get networks running faster.

The deployment accelerators are described as simplifying site access, device onboarding, and connectivity management. Two of them, TowerX and CatalyX, are named on the solutions page. A partner program helps utilities integrate devices, applications, and network components so deployments move faster. That program spans over 150 technology providers, from rugged device manufacturers to software companies, with solutions validated for 900 MHz networks.

Eleven utility customers are deploying its 900 MHz solutions, the company states. It describes itself as the largest holder of licensed 900 MHz spectrum in the United States, counting the contiguous states plus Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico. The about page also claims over 93% of Texas counties served. The same page traces the founders back to Nextel.

before.description: Interconnection and grid capacity workflow software for utilities and ISOs - exhibited at DISTRIBUTECH 2026

paragraphs: GridUnity sells software for transmission and distribution interconnection, aimed at making energy project approvals faster. It is built for the parties on both sides of an interconnection request, including ISOs, RTOs, utilities, developers and transmission owners.

The platform runs the life cycle from application intake to commissioning in one place. It is delivered as configurable software as a service, which the company says lets customers meet federal and state orders as those evolve. Near real-time data sharing among developers, utilities and regulators is offered as a way to cut disputes and speed studies. The company states compliance with NIST 800-171 and SOC 2 Type II standards.

Products are broken out for transmission, for large load and for distribution. On its own record the company cites a five-year research and development strategy focused on AI, automation and predictive analytics. It also cites $45 million in matching Department of Energy funding and GRIP award recognition. Collaboration with research institutions and government agencies is described as part of that work.

paragraphs: Tantalus is a technology company selling grid modernization systems to public power and electric cooperative utilities. It has been delivering data-centric products to that market for more than 35 years.

The products sit on the Tantalus Grid Modernization Platform, a modular architecture meant to move data across devices, systems and vendors. One piece is edge-computing metering infrastructure aimed at resiliency, reliability and lower total cost of ownership. Another handles load management and distributed energy resources sitting behind the meter. A gateway device fits any ANSI meter socket and adds visibility and control behind the meter without replacing the meter itself.

Utilities across North America partner with the company on distribution grid work, with published case studies including one in Bolivar, Tennessee. Tantalus Systems trades on the TSX under the symbol GRID and on OTCQX. It is based in Burnaby, British Columbia. Recent announcements include a debt restructuring and an annual survey of how utilities view grid modernization.

paragraphs: Cyclomedia sells geospatial data built from street-level imagery, lidar point clouds, and aerial data covering public space. Public authorities are a core market, using it to manage streets, buildings, and public assets. Utility and energy providers use it to plan, inspect, and manage their networks.

Street Smart, the company's viewer, brings 360 degree imagery, lidar, and map layers into one browser-based workspace. From the desk, users measure distances along facades, pavements, and openings. Automated analysis detects pavement defects, surface types, and deterioration in high-resolution imagery. Property valuation is another stated use, supported by current visual evidence and measurements. Open integrations and APIs connect the data to existing GIS and asset management systems.

The company says it has worked in geospatial capture and visualisation for more than 40 years with public authorities across Europe and beyond. Specialised capture vehicles survey cities and regions throughout the year. Routes are coordinated with local authorities to limit disruption. Its case studies page lists a digital twin created for the London Borough of Harrow from street imagery and lidar.

paragraphs: CyberLock, Inc. sells a key-centric electronic access control system meant to increase security, accountability and key control across an organization. Its electronic cylinders retrofit into existing door hardware without power or wiring.

Because the wire between the lock and the managing software is eliminated, locks can be installed almost anywhere. The company describes the result as the convenience of a mechanical key system plus the access permission and tracking of an electronic one. Key control cabinets automatically program and dispense the smart keys. A patented FlashLock option provides keyless access control from a smartphone, tablet or iPad.

Stated uses include airports, where the system can secure hangars, perimeter and interior gates, baggage and restricted areas. Water and power utilities are another, covering substations, reservoirs, equipment and storage areas. Corporate uses listed run to classrooms, computer carts and employee and student files. paragraphs: IQGeo gives telecom and utility operators a single platform to plan, design, build, and operate their physical network infrastructure. It is aimed at telecom, fiber, and utility network operators, including planners, engineers, and construction teams.

Network Manager Telecom is built to plan, build, and operate fiber and coax networks with accurate data, simple field tools, and automated AI quality checks. Field staff can download their work area, update records offline, and sync changes back automatically. Construction photos are audited with real-time visual AI to verify quality, completeness, and compliance at scale. A companion product, Network Manager Electric, is described as built for geospatial work execution, combining geospatial intelligence with AI-powered workflows across the full lifecycle.

Buyers choose between two deployment options, an IQGeo SaaS deployment or a private cloud deployment they host themselves. The hosted option is listed with ISO/IEC 27001:2013 certification. The private cloud option is pitched at operators needing bespoke integration with legacy GIS and OSS/BSS systems. The company says electric and gas utilities rely on it for asset management, grid modernization, inspection and field operations. On the telecom side it describes its customers as reaching some of the largest and fastest-growing global telecom operators, managing highly complex, rapidly scaling networks.

For fire professionals, it aims to equip emergency managers and first responders to optimize response efforts, improve coordination, and protect firefighter safety. before.name: LineVision
before.description: Non-contact transmission line monitoring and dynamic line ratings for utilities - exhibited at DISTRIBUTECH 2026

paragraphs: LineVision sells an integrated intelligence platform that delivers Dynamic Line Ratings and Situational Awareness for transmission networks. Dynamic Line Ratings covers real-time and forecasted transmission capacity at every span across networks. Forecasted ratings extend hourly up to 240 hours, or 10 days. Items listed under Dynamic Line Ratings include FERC 881 and NERC FAC-008 compliance.

Situational Awareness provides real-time monitoring of physical risks and environmental conditions on critical transmission lines. That monitoring runs on RS-1 sensors that gather continuous, hyperlocal data around critical transmission rights-of-way. Detection and alerting cover conductor hazards including galloping, clashing, asynchronous motion, and unusual sag. Other alerts listed cover conductor icing, fallen trees, and unauthorized people or equipment in the ROW.

LineVision states that it works with 7 to the 10 largest utilities in the US. Named customers on these pages include National Grid, Xcel Energy, Avangrid, and New York Transco. Service capabilities listed include 24/7 customer support for operational DLR and EMS integration described as NERC-CIP compliant. The home page states that LineVision solutions are US-domiciled and NERC-CIP approved, with the SMS certified to ISO 27001:2022.

before.name: SmartWorks

paragraphs: SmartWorks sells SmartWorks Compass, a platform that helps electric, water, and gas utilities improve data accuracy, automate operational workflows, and uncover insight through analytics and AI. The platform covers data management, operational intelligence, analytics, automation, and AI capabilities, and its modular structure lets a utility begin with one priority and add capabilities as requirements change. Compass is built to sit alongside systems a utility already runs, and SmartWorks integrates with CIS, AMI, AMR, customer engagement, and other utility environments.

SmartWorks Athena is the AI line, letting utility staff explore operational information in everyday language rather than through custom reports or technical queries. Athena reaches meter-to-cash, AMI, CIS, and operational data through plain-English questions, and it can also support compatible CIS and MDM environments outside SmartWorks Compass.

SmartWorks Connect is a separate portal line that utilities use to give residential and commercial customers self-service access, usage insights, billing details, alerts, and service tools. These pages name electric, water, gas, and multi-commodity utilities as the customers for all of it, and place that work across North America and the Caribbean. The company describes itself as part of Harris Utilities, working alongside established CIS, customer engagement, and complementary utility technology providers.

before.name: AiDash
before.description: Satellite + AI vegetation management (IVMS) and climate/asset risk SaaS for utilities - exhibited at DISTRIBUTECH 2026

paragraphs: AiDASH sells software that electric utilities use to find vegetation, asset, wildfire and storm risk before it takes the grid down. The method starts with continuous satellite monitoring, then adds targeted aerial, vehicle-mounted and on-demand inspection.

Very high resolution satellite passes refresh vegetation health data up to twelve times a year. Higher-cadence imagery tracks fuel load, moisture and burnability up to seven times a week. One system covers asset inspection and monitoring. Another handles wildfire situational awareness and risk mitigation. A storm system predicts outages 120 hours ahead so crews can be pre-positioned. The platform exposes REST APIs for automation or for integrating with systems a utility already runs.

The company says it was founded by serial entrepreneurs in 2019. Its about page claims more than 150 customers of every size around the world. The platform page states SOC 2 Type 2 certification. A news item on the site announces that Schneider Electric agreed to acquire AiDASH for $350 million.

paragraphs: AiDASH sells software that electric utilities use to find vegetation, asset, wildfire and storm risk before it takes the grid down. The method starts with continuous satellite monitoring, then adds targeted aerial, vehicle-mounted and on-demand inspection.

Very high resolution satellite passes refresh vegetation health data up to twelve times a year. Higher-cadence imagery tracks fuel load, moisture and burnability up to seven times a week. One system covers asset inspection and monitoring. Another handles wildfire situational awareness and risk mitigation. A storm system predicts outages 120 hours ahead so crews can be pre-positioned. The platform exposes REST APIs for automation or for integrating with systems a utility already runs.

The company says it was founded by serial entrepreneurs in 2019. Its about page claims more than 150 customers of every size around the world. The platform page states SOC 2 Type 2 certification. A news item on the site announces that Schneider Electric agreed to acquire AiDASH for $350 million.

paragraphs: Activu makes software for control rooms and command centers, the places where operators watch incidents unfold together in real time. The company describes its product as a network-based visual intelligence software solution for mission-critical operations. It also designs, builds, and supports the rooms themselves, including security operations centers, fusion centers, and video walls.

The platform, called vis/ability, serves real time crime centers, emergency operations centers, and other security operations centers. One listed addition is active shooter recognition. paragraphs: Skydio makes autonomous drones, along with the docks and software to run them, and sells drone programs to customers from energy networks to neighborhood precincts to battlefields. Those programs cover Drone as First Responder, automated inspection and site security. Dock for X10 positions Skydio X10 drones at a site so that missions launch remotely without anyone present. The smaller Skydio R10 puts eyes indoors before officers enter.

Skydio states that more than 1,500 public safety agencies use its drones. In a Drone as First Responder program, Skydio says its drones launch in under 20 seconds and reach incidents autonomously in under 90 seconds. DFR Command is the software from which remote operators launch and manage drones, respond to multiple calls and stream live video to patrol and command. It integrates with RapidSOS and CAD at dispatch, Axon Fusus for live operations, and automatic evidence upload into Axon Evidence. Skydio's customer stories include Brookhaven PD, which it says reached 30 second response times after deploying 8 Docks.

Skydio Site Security uses the same dock-based drones to verify alarms, patrol perimeters and deliver live visibility across a site. Video streams into Genetec or Milestone, and flights launch automatically when triggered by alarms or access control events. Skydio says its data is encrypted in transit and at rest and that it aligns to SOC 2, ISO 27001 and NIST frameworks.

paragraphs: FLASHNET sells inteliLIGHT, a remote management system for street lighting made up of lamp controllers and software. The customers it names are city managers, street lighting operators and lamp manufacturers around the world.

Controllers are built for both individual lamp and lighting segment control. City examples on the home page run over NB-IoT and cellular communications. The company page puts energy savings at up to 35 percent through smart dimming scheduling, with overall operational costs down by up to 42 percent. The system is presented as compatible with major smart city standards.

It says that since 2005 more than 400 million people have seen the benefits of inteliLIGHT, in hundreds of cities on six continents. The company has been part of Lucy Group since 2022.

paragraphs: EPIC iO sells AI-driven monitoring for physical sites, along with the wireless connectivity that keeps those locations online. Its named settings are utilities, oil and gas, construction, retail and industrial sites. Both sides run on a software platform the company calls EPIC Cortex.

The video analysis is meant to separate security events from environmental activity such as weather or wildlife, which cuts false alarms. License plate recognition adds vehicle awareness at site entrances, along the perimeter and for vehicle activity on site. For police use, the LPR page says the system alerts officers and dispatchers within seconds. On the connectivity side, the company offers primary, backup and failover links across 5G, satellite and fixed networks. The same platform centralizes SIM and device management across multiple carriers with real-time usage monitoring.

For public safety and critical infrastructure customers, EPIC iO frames its role as situational awareness that supports emergency response without replacing established response protocols. Homepage testimonials are attributed anonymously, by role, to bodies such as a municipal public safety agency. The about page names an AI platform called DeepInsights as the cornerstone of its mission.

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently" The URL is factually correct and does NOT violate the parent-domain rule: aws.amazon.com is AWS's own canonical property (its own brand, console, pricing, docs and its own careers page at https://aws.amazon.com/careers/, HTTP 200), not Amazon's corporate site at amazon.com. The govtech tie is on-domain too: https://aws.amazon.com/government-education/ (HTTP 200) is AWS's public sector page, and the homepage names 'AWS GovCloud (US-East)' and 'AWS GovCloud (US-West)'. MY JUDGMENT ON WHETHER THE BOARD SHOULD CARRY THIS AT ALL - the URL passes but the record is still risky, for a reason the URL check cannot fix: aws.amazon.com/careers/ does not host jobs, it hands off to https://www.amazon.jobs/en/business_categories/amazon-web-services. That feed is tens of thousands of global AWS engineering/PM/ops roles, of which SLED account executive roles are a tiny fraction. Any homepage- or careers-page-level scrape of this record will flood SLED JOBS with irrelevant listings - the same practical damage the parent-domain rule exists to prevent, arriving by a different route. Recommendation: keep the URL if AWS is wanted on the board, but the record must be wired to

paragraphs: Neara sells physics-based digital twin software to electric utilities, which use it to model their networks. The pitch is to unify assets, surroundings and workflows in a single physics-accurate view.

The model is built from a utility's existing LiDAR, imagery, GIS and asset records. Teams then simulate wind, ice, thermal, flood, vegetation, reconductoring and new builds on the real network geometry. Outputs include prioritized hardening plans, regulator-ready reports and field-ready work orders. Solution areas cover resiliency and reliability, wildfire mitigation, asset management, risk and value optimization, and design and construction.

On the asset side, replacement candidates are ranked by measured load rather than by install date. Wildfire work pulls pole loading, asset condition, vegetation, GIS accuracy, weather and consequence into one physics-backed model. Resiliency work prioritizes mitigation by how asset condition, vegetation proximity and environmental conditions interact across the network. Case study quotes on the site are attributed to the chief executive of Essential Energy. Another comes from a general manager of network management at SA Power Networks.

quote.text: Utilities on four continents run their networks on Neara, from ambitious regional co-ops to national grid operators.

paragraphs: Itron sells metering and grid technology for electricity, gas and water, and its homepage names utilities and cities as the customers it builds for. The product menu separates smart electricity management, smart gas management and smart water solutions, with advanced metering infrastructure and meter data management listed underneath. Network and software offerings sit beside the meters, among them communication networks, distribution automation, grid edge management and distributed energy resource management.

A partner locator publishes third party products that connect to Itron networks, including a battery powered natural gas alarm listed as compatible with one of them. Those listed products include street lighting controllers, power quality monitoring, underground cable monitoring and traffic detection.

paragraphs: Boston Dynamics builds mobile robots that companies use to automate tedious and hazardous work in manufacturing, logistics and other industries. Its product line covers Spot, Stretch, Atlas and Orbit. Spot is a mobile robot that automates sensing and inspection and captures data wherever it is sent. The company states that over 1,500 Spot robots are in customer hands today.

Spot works on factory floors, construction sites and research labs. As a sensing platform it gives teams insight into routine operations, site health or potentially hazardous situations. In energy and natural resources it performs inspections in energized, radioactive or otherwise hazardous areas. Operators can also use it to remotely investigate, assess and de-escalate tense or hazardous situations, reducing the risk to personnel. With the Spot Arm, operators can handle tasks such as nuclear material handling or suspicious package investigation from a safe distance. Standard payload configurations cover inspection, public safety and innovation, including a Government & Public Safety Kit.

Stretch, the company's warehouse robot, handles cases and unloads trailers. Orbit, its fleet management software, manages autonomous tasks, operates robots remotely and analyzes data within the context of a facility map. Atlas, a humanoid robot, is in early field testing with Hyundai on real-world sequencing tasks. The company has announced a new 323,000 square foot facility in Waltham, Massachusetts.

paragraphs: Bidgely builds energy analytics software for electric utilities, working from the data their smart meters already collect. The core claim is that a utility can identify what is running inside every home and business from meter data alone, with no surveys or smart plugs.

The platform, called UtilityAI, breaks that meter signal down to appliance level for every customer, grid asset and hour of the year. Utilities use it on the customer side to resolve high bill questions before people call in. On the grid side it is pitched for capacity planning that accounts for distributed energy resources. Program teams are offered targeting for EV and electrification enrollment. There is also a module for discovering and remedying energy theft. The company offers the software as SaaS or deployed inside a utility's own cloud.

Buyers span the utility enterprise, covering customer experience, grid operations and efficiency and electrification programs. Case studies on the site report results such as 238% of contracted savings in the first year of a deployment. Bidgely also runs an annual conference, registration for which is advertised on the home page.

before.name: Camus Energy
before.description: Grid orchestration and DER management for municipal utilities and co-ops - exhibited at DISTRIBUTECH 2026

paragraphs: Camus Energy sells software that electric utilities use to interconnect data centers and local generation. What it sells is the flexible grid connection, in which the utility guarantees firm capacity for most of a site's demand and applies conditional limits to the rest.

Camus uses real utility data to map how much additional load each conductor and substation can safely serve in every hour of the year. Utilities then decide what portion of the load is served firmly and set operating limits for the conditional portion. Day-ahead operating forecasts show when those conditional limits will apply, alongside closed loop controls. The platform pulls SCADA data, GIS assets, network models, AMI, and DER telemetry into one consistent system model. Two applications sit on it: FlexConnect for interconnections and ODMS, which gives utilities a unified view of the distribution grid.

The company says it supports investor-owned and public power utilities. It counts 12 or more utility partners across the United States. It states that joint studies with Google, AES, and Princeton's ZERO Lab set the benchmark for how utilities and developers evaluate flexibility and grid capacity. On security, it says OAuth authentication, MFA, role-based access, audit logging, and continuous monitoring protect the platform.

paragraphs: KloudGin sells work and asset management software to water and wastewater utilities. Gas utilities are a second market for the same platform. Municipalities and other public sector agencies are a third.

One part of the platform handles construction work management for complex projects, built on utility industry expertise. An enterprise asset management side unifies assets and workforce to optimize operations. Work management gives crews a view of assets, work orders, records and AI-native decision support. Prebuilt modules cover specific utility jobs such as automating fire hydrant maintenance. Others handle 811 ticket automation for dig requests. Another helps crews identify, document and replace lead service lines. GIS capabilities are embedded to support location-based customer service, and a separate adapter serves SAP customers.

An IDC MarketScape evaluation cited on the site names the company a Leader in utilities enterprise asset management. The company has announced a partnership with Black & Veatch. Its chief executive is named on the site as Vikram Takru. It also positions itself as a platform choice for cities.

paragraphs: Accruent sells software for managing buildings, spaces and physical assets across every stage of real estate, facilities and asset management. The stated aim is to run the full lifecycle of assets and facilities with connected workflows and reporting behind it.

paragraphs: Virtual Peaker sells cloud software that lets an electric utility reach the smart devices already sitting in homes and businesses and use them to shave peak load and cost. The buyers are utilities standing up demand response programs.

Three suites make up the product, and the company presents them together as a virtual power plant platform that aggregates distributed energy resources at the edge of the grid. The Shift suite is the dispatch side, aggregating resources at homes and at commercial and industrial sites to hold down peak market costs and defer new construction. The Relay suite handles the customer side, signing people up and paying out the incentives. A utility can run several program types at once across electric vehicles, thermostats, water heaters and batteries.

The company describes partnerships with more than thirty device types, from thermostats to electric vehicle chargers. It states that the platform is SOC 2 Type 2 certified. Municipal energy providers are named as one audience, using demand response to meet grid goals and engage customers. One published case study covers Sacramento Municipal Utility District optimizing hot water heater efficiency on the platform.

paragraphs: Fulcrum sells a field operations platform that organizations use to run, record and close out work done away from an office. The pitch is aimed at teams still working from paper forms and a scatter of separate point tools.

Crews are given location-enabled apps on ordinary mobile devices in place of paperwork. They capture points, lines and polygons using the device's own GPS or a Bluetooth receiver. The collected records move into ArcGIS or other systems through APIs and formats such as shapefiles and GeoJSON. The company treats working without a signal as a baseline rather than an add-on.

State and local government is one of the named audiences, alongside utilities, construction and public works, with inspections and documentation for community projects. The home page states nearly 3,000 companies and 50,000 users in over 100 countries. On security, the company points to SCIM and SOC 2 compliance, and its timeline records an independent SOC 2 Type 1 certification. Spatial Networks Inc. is named as the maker of Fulcrum, and the company reports acquiring Wildnote to deepen environmental compliance work.

paragraphs: Overstory sells vegetation intelligence to electric utilities, from investor-owned utilities to municipalities and cooperatives. The analysis rests on satellite imagery, which in one European project was used to identify 37 species of vegetation.

The company notes that vegetation management is typically a utility's greatest operations budget item. Its pitch is spending less on unnecessary trimming and more on riskier areas. Utilities can see strike trees, declining trees and hazard trees individually or aggregated. Encroachment risk, hazard trees and species identification can be laid over wildfire risk maps to show where trimming matters most. The same data lets a utility verify and document risk reduction from work that contractors completed.

Risk reports are meant to support data-driven conversations with regulators, insurers and executives. Indra den Bakker and Anniek Schouten founded the company in Lisbon in 2018. The company says it has worked with more than 50 investor-owned utilities and cooperatives across the Americas and Europe.

paragraphs: Anterix provides private 900 MHz spectrum to utilities so they can run their own wireless networks instead of leaning on commercial carriers. The company frames that as operational control, with the utility owning the communications infrastructure behind essential services. Licensed spectrum is sold together with deployment solutions and ecosystem partners so utilities can get networks running faster.

The deployment accelerators are described as simplifying site access, device onboarding, and connectivity management. Two of them, TowerX and CatalyX, are named on the solutions page. It describes itself as the largest holder of licensed 900 MHz spectrum in the United States, counting the contiguous states plus Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico. before.name: Heimdall Power
before.description: Dynamic line rating sensors (Neuron) for transmission utilities - exhibited at DISTRIBUTECH 2026

paragraphs: Heimdall Power sells sensors and software to electric utilities, with capacity tools meant to help them safely adjust transmission limits, improve operational planning and stay compliant with industry standards. The company was founded in Norway in 2016.

Its dynamic line rating offering combines physical and virtual Neurons to take real-time, on-line measurements. The sensors report temperature, current and inclination on the conductor. Deployment is handled by an autonomous drone installation system that the company says places Neurons in remote or hard-to-reach areas. A facility ratings module consolidates all ratings into one unified system and is aimed at simplifying NERC FAC-008 compliance. Further tools give grid operators real-time visibility into threats like icing, line movement, electrical faults and wildfire risks.

The about page states that the company has grown 10x in two years, raised a $25M Series B and expanded with a North American headquarters in Charlotte, NC. A news item on the site reports that Heimdall Power was selected by Statnett for a new Dynamic Line Rating project.

before.name: Technosylva
before.description: Wildfire spread modeling and risk analytics used by CAL FIRE and major utilities - exhibited at DISTRIBUTECH 2026

paragraphs: Technosylva sells wildfire and extreme weather risk software to electric utilities and fire agencies. The point of it is turning complicated weather data into something a planning or response team can act on.

For planning, the company combines large numbers of validated fire simulations with historical weather and a customer's own asset data. Its models estimate what an ignition would mean in acres burned, buildings destroyed and people affected. For operations, simulations run nightly to produce the wildfire risk metrics crews plan around. Utilities use the output to target power shutoffs instead of cutting service broadly. Feeds from computer-aided dispatch and IRWIN bring in incidents from federal and state agencies. Flooding, high wind, extreme temperature and winter storms sit in the same view as fire.
The homepage points readers toward Xcel Energy, CAL FIRE and CORE. Bryan Spear is named as chief executive. The company has also announced modeling of urban conflagration in the built environment.

paragraphs: Aurigo Software sells capital program management software to government agencies that plan, build and maintain public infrastructure. It also serves facility owners in areas such as data centers, life sciences, manufacturing, and energy and utilities. The company's platform, Masterworks, brings planning, execution, financials, right of way and analytics together in one system.

On the delivery side it coordinates contracts, schedules, costs and field work so teams can hold to the original plan and keep a complete audit trail. Compliance, funding transparency and governance are meant to sit inside everyday work so public money stays accountable. Agencies can change forms, workflows, business rules and dashboards through configuration rather than code. An AI layer called Lumina supports decision-making with compliance and governance built in, and the company says every insight and recommendation it produces can be audited and traced.

Cities, counties, transit agencies and transportation departments across North America use the platform to manage capital programs, replace legacy systems and automate federal reimbursements. The company claims more than 300 customers and over 20 years of capital program expertise behind the product. It also says the software monitors project signals to catch cost, schedule and delivery risks before they turn critical.

before.name: Daupler
before.description: After-hours call intake, incident triage and crew dispatch software for water, sewer and electric utilities and public works departments - exhibited at AWWA ACE 2026, DISTRIBUTECH 2026

paragraphs: Daupler sells a response management system that gives teams the information and tools to respond to service requests and emergencies. Public works, utilities, and service organizations of all sizes are named as the users. The work runs from odor complaints to water main breaks.

The company runs call centers that take intake calls, notify staff about urgent issues, and document noncritical calls for the next day. An automated roster callout feature forms crews without anyone working a phone list by hand. Event detection spots incidents affecting multiple people and stops repeat calls from being dispatched. For outbound messages, the system sends a text or a recorded voice message depending on whether the number is mobile or a landline. The platform sits at the center of existing information systems and combines their data into one view of an incident. Site arrival times and crew check-ins are logged to help make sure crews get back safely.
The company states clients are seeing a 20-75% reduction in callouts. Its pages describe the City of Durham integrating the system with CityWorks.

before.name: ImageTrend
before.description: Incident records and ePCR data platform for EMS and fire agencies - exhibited at IAFC FRI 2026

paragraphs: ImageTrend sells software that fire departments, EMS agencies, and hospitals run their emergency response operations on. Its core product is ePCR software built for how medics actually work, with AI-assisted documentation, configurable workflows, and real-time intelligence for agencies at any scale.

The platform connects scheduling, documentation, compliance, unified analytics, operational readiness, and hospital data exchange in one system. NEMSIS, NERIS, NTDB, and TQIP compliance is built into every workflow, with software filling and validating fields while staff review and confirm before submission. A scheduling product, ImageTrend Slate, addresses the demands of EMS, fire departments, and other critical services. It manages time-off requests, shift trades, and employee availability. Separate pre-plan software digitizes floor plans, hazard locations, water supply points, and utility shutoffs so responders have instant access to tactical data on scene.

The company reports 9,000 agencies, 43 state repositories, and more than a billion records processed. It says its sales engineering team is entirely former fire and EMS. It cites 24/7 US-based support and a 96.5% satisfaction rate, backed by 25 years in the field.

before.name: Tablet Command
before.description: Mobile incident command and response for fire/EMS departments - exhibited at IAFC FRI 2026

paragraphs: Tablet Command makes mobile incident command and response software for fire and EMS agencies. Commanders run an incident on a digital command board, dragging and dropping unit assignments.

The software is built on the iPad platform. A commander can tap and drag responding apparatus onto a scene, track progress against critical checklists, and time-stamp every maneuver and benchmark. Maps carry pre-plans and custom layers for hydrants, hospitals, landing zones, flood hazards and fire trails. The app is native and designed to run entirely independent of internet connectivity. It connects to CAD systems and integrates Esri GIS map layers, pre-plans, FireMapper and AVL.

The site reports over 250,000 incidents managed, covering everyday calls and multi-agency coordination. The product is also positioned as a complete replacement for mobile data terminals in the fire service. San Bernardino County Fire is named as using it in every front line response unit. A case study describes Stockton Fire Department turning to it as an MDT replacement and fire ground accountability tool.

before.description: Digital dashboards and signage for public safety - exhibited at IACP 2026, IAFC FRI 2026

paragraphs: First Arriving sells a real-time information platform that connects the critical systems an agency already runs. The site claims 1400+ Fire, EMS, Law Enforcement & Local Government Agencies as users. The same information shows up at the station on the big screen, in the office on a desktop, and on a tablet in the field.

The platform centralizes data from 130+ systems into one operational view. Connected sources include CAD, RMS, staffing, fleet, facilities, GIS, scheduling, training, and alerts. Alerts can be pushed with required acknowledgments so the right people act immediately. Individual user accounts and role-based views mean each member of a team sees what they need.

The law enforcement version is designed for police departments, sheriff's offices, campus safety, and agencies of all sizes. It carries things like daily shift briefings and watch commander notes. A local government version covers council meetings, facility schedules, emergency alerts, and public notices. Lobbies, public counters and reception areas are named as display locations. The company notes that its marketing division is now ResponderMAX.
