notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "© AT&T Intellectual Property. All rights reserved. FirstNet and the FirstNet logo are registered trademarks and service marks of the First Responder Network Authority." Fetched https://www.firstnet.com. The entity question in the CAUTION resolves cleanly: the footer copyright is AT&T's ('© AT&T Intellectual Property'), while the FirstNet marks are acknowledged as belonging to the First Responder Network Authority — i.e. this domain is the AT&T-operated commercial service, which is exactly the board entity 'FirstNet, Built with AT&T'. I confirmed the split by also fetching the federal side: firstnetauthority.gov states 'The First Responder Network Authority is an independent agency within the U.S. Department of Commerce's National Telecommunications and Information Administration' and sends users elsewhere for service with 'Access my FirstNet account (FirstNet.com).' So .gov is the agency, .com is the AT&T service. On rule 3: firstnet.com is NOT the parent's corporate domain (that is att.com) — it is the product's own dedicated domain with its own branding, plans and support, so it is acceptable. FLAG for the board operator, though: FirstNet does not recruit as a separate employer. Sales roles on this product are posted as AT&T requisitions, so a scraper pointed at firstnet.com will like

paragraphs: FirstNet is a wireless network built with and for the public safety community. Agencies can buy service for their teams. Individual public service professionals who pay for their own service can sign up too.

Traffic rides Band 14, described as a separate lane for time on duty or on call. Calls, texts and data always receive First Priority on the network. Phones, tablets and other hardware are certified for FirstNet before they are sold on it. Cell boosters, routers and repeaters sit alongside those handsets. So do deployables and satellite options for places where coverage falls short.

Eligibility runs across healthcare, public works, the justice system, the National Guard and more. paragraphs: LeoSight describes a unified command platform that connects law enforcement, fire, EMS, and emergency management across jurisdictions. The platform integrates CAD, cameras, ALPR, drones/DFR, gunshot acoustic detection, and field systems into one connected operational network. A second function covers cross-agency communication and shared workflows, from the initial call through investigation and case closure.

Agencies building a command center and agencies just getting started are both named, across law enforcement, fire, EMS, and emergency services.

before.name: Miovision
before.description: Traffic data collection and smart intersection technology - exhibited at IAFC FRI 2026, APTA 2026

paragraphs: Miovision sells traffic data collection tools meant to give planners the accurate, verifiable data their mobility plans depend on. It also sells detection equipment that improves signal performance by responding to real-world road user demand, from bicycles to articulated trucks. Its Opticom line clears the path for emergency fleets without re-timing entire corridors.

Portable devices capture comprehensive multimodal count data including cars, trucks, pedestrians and bikes. A newer optimization product replaces manual five-year retiming cycles with iterative, objective-based optimization that the company says cuts manual effort by up to half. Engineers compare plans side-by-side, validate against industry standards, and push updates directly to field controllers without manual data re-entry.

The company says that since 2005 it has had 2,000 customers in 68 countries and 13,000 cities, with 30 billion vehicles and 1.5 billion pedestrians counted. It lists more than 300 detection customers in North America. Detroit partnered with Miovision to upgrade over 600 intersections. In San Rafael, police and fire vehicles now receive signal priority at 53 intersections.

paragraphs: Flock Safety sells license plate readers, video cameras, gunshot detection and response drones to law enforcement agencies, schools, businesses and neighborhoods to help them deter crime, respond to emergencies and investigate safety incidents. Its license plate recognition cameras capture plates and vehicle characteristics such as make, color and body type to generate investigative leads. Responders get an instant alert when a vehicle matches a customer-defined or NCIC hot list. Users include law enforcement agencies, businesses, neighborhoods, apartment complexes, houses of worship and schools.

Beyond plate readers, Flock sells PTZ video cameras for open areas such as parking lots, intersections and parks, and fixed cameras for buildings and city streets. A gunshot and audio detection product verifies gunfire and links each alert with nearby LPR reads and video. Flock DFR, its drone as first responder system, launches a docked drone to the coordinates of a 911 call, LPR hit or gunshot alert and streams live video to officers before they arrive. Solar-powered mobile trailers cover parking lots, retail centers and construction sites, and an optional Alert Response Service puts trained agents on live alerts.

Flock sells on an annual subscription that covers hardware, software, maintenance and support. The company has reduced its recommended default data retention from 30 days to 7 days, which it says applies to new law enforcement customers. Customers control their data and how it is shared, and every search is logged.

Responders get an instant alert when a vehicle matches a customer-defined or NCIC hot list. Users include law enforcement agencies, businesses, neighborhoods, apartment complexes, houses of worship and schools.

Beyond plate readers, Flock sells PTZ video cameras for open areas such as parking lots, intersections and parks, and fixed cameras for buildings and city streets. A gunshot and audio detection product verifies gunfire and links each alert with nearby LPR reads and video. Flock DFR, its drone as first responder system, launches a docked drone to the coordinates of a 911 call, LPR hit or gunshot alert and streams live video to officers before they arrive. Solar-powered mobile trailers cover parking lots, retail centers and construction sites, and an optional Alert Response Service puts trained agents on live alerts.

Flock sells on an annual subscription that covers hardware, software, maintenance and support. The company has reduced its recommended default data retention from 30 days to 7 days, which it says applies to new law enforcement customers. Customers control their data and how it is shared, and every search is logged.

paragraphs: Peregrine builds what it calls Operational AI for High-Criticality Organizations. Law enforcement is listed as a solution area, and the platform is positioned for public safety work.

A banner on the site announces a $250 million Series D.

before.description: Fire trucks, aerials and rescue apparatus for fire departments

paragraphs: E-ONE manufactures custom, heavy-duty fire trucks. The line covers pumpers, tankers, aerial ladders and platforms, rescues, industrial units and aircraft rescue and firefighting vehicles. Those trucks reach fire departments through a dealer network.

The company was founded in 1974 by an industrial engineer and says it designed and manufactured the first modular, extruded aluminum fire truck and body. A company timeline runs from that first modular all-aluminum body through decades of chassis, ladders and platforms. The same timeline records testing cabs in excess of the European ECE-R29 crash worthiness standard. Recent entries include an all-electric fire truck called the Vector.

E-ONE writes that first responders and the communities they serve have relied on it for 50 years. The timeline notes that American Industrial Partners purchased the company. Company news reports an order from the Chicago Fire Department for 120 emergency vehicles from E-ONE and Wheeled Coach. Another post describes a $23.5 million expansion expected to increase aerial production by 35 percent and add 100 new jobs in Ocala.

paragraphs: Extra Duty Solutions administers extra duty programs for public safety agencies such as police departments, sheriff offices, state agencies, and fire departments. It also gives law enforcement agencies access to public safety scheduling software from Jivasoft, its IT division. Today it provides scheduling software and administrative support for agencies across the country.

The about page dates the business to 2015, when it served large corporations and coordinated extra-duty officers for executive protection, factory security, and logistics needs. In 2016 the focus shifted to serving the agencies themselves. In 2017 the company exited the corporate market entirely, which it says removed the conflict of interest that arises when one firm represents both the agency and the corporate customer.

Extra Duty Solutions acquired Jivasoft, a Texas-based company in law enforcement scheduling software, which brought the On-Duty and Xtra-Duty platforms into its lineup. Milestones listed on the same page include initiating service with a 100th agency. Later entries record surpassing $150M in annualized extra-duty invoicing. The most recent listed milestone is a 250th agency partnership. According to its own news release, the company was ranked No. 2740 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of fastest-growing private companies in America.

paragraphs: Esri builds ArcGIS, its geographic information system software for mapping and spatial analysis. The company describes itself as the global market leader in GIS software, location intelligence, and mapping. Its stated audience is business, government, and society.

ArcGIS is presented as enterprise technology that integrates and connects data through the context of geography. The premise is that hidden patterns, trends, and relationships emerge once data is visualized and analyzed on a map. Beyond maps and analysis, the company says its technology speeds data sharing and collaboration. For agencies that want to keep everything in house, there is a self-hosted edition for mapping, analytics, and data management.

Esri says it has supported customers with geographic science and geospatial analytics since 1969. Officials working in public safety, transportation, infrastructure, health and human services, and other fields use the technology to support high-level decisions. At the local level, the company says community leaders apply it to economic development, public works, and urban planning. Published stories include the US Census Bureau modernizing its entire census process with GIS.

ArcGIS is presented as enterprise technology that integrates and connects data through the context of geography. The premise is that hidden patterns, trends, and relationships emerge once data is visualized and analyzed on a map. Beyond maps and analysis, the company says its technology speeds data sharing and collaboration. For agencies that want to keep everything in house, there is a self-hosted edition for mapping, analytics, and data management.

Esri says it has supported customers with geographic science and geospatial analytics since 1969. Officials working in public safety, transportation, infrastructure, health and human services, and other fields use the technology to support high-level decisions. At the local level, the company says community leaders apply it to economic development, public works, and urban planning. Published stories include the US Census Bureau modernizing its entire census process with GIS.

paragraphs: HAAS Alert sells a collision prevention service that sends real-time digital alerts warning drivers about nearby emergency vehicles and roadway hazards. Its customers are fleets that work at the roadside, including tow trucks, utility vehicles, waste management trucks, school buses and snowplows.

The system is wired to a vehicle's warning light bar or master switch, so alerting begins when crews turn on their lights and stops when they turn them off. Motorists install nothing, because alerts are broadcast directly to the navigation platforms they already use. Fleets can activate the service through three primary methods, depending on their existing setup. The company says drivers get up to 30 seconds of advance warning to slow down and move over.

The company traces its start to 2015, when co-founder and CEO Cory Hohs was almost struck by an ambulance on the road. He co-founded the business with Noah Levens and Jigar Patel. Its timeline notes that the United States Department of Homeland Security awarded $1.1 million toward development for digital alerting. It also states that digital alerting was codified and funded in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

paragraphs: Skydio makes autonomous drones, along with the docks and software to run them, and sells drone programs to customers from energy networks to neighborhood precincts to battlefields. Those programs cover Drone as First Responder, automated inspection and site security. Dock for X10 positions Skydio X10 drones at a site so that missions launch remotely without anyone present. The smaller Skydio R10 puts eyes indoors before officers enter.

Skydio states that more than 1,500 public safety agencies use its drones. In a Drone as First Responder program, Skydio says its drones launch in under 20 seconds and reach incidents autonomously in under 90 seconds. DFR Command is the software from which remote operators launch and manage drones, respond to multiple calls and stream live video to patrol and command. It integrates with RapidSOS and CAD at dispatch, Axon Fusus for live operations, and automatic evidence upload into Axon Evidence. Skydio's customer stories include Brookhaven PD, which it says reached 30 second response times after deploying 8 Docks.

Skydio Site Security uses the same dock-based drones to verify alarms, patrol perimeters and deliver live visibility across a site. Video streams into Genetec or Milestone, and flights launch automatically when triggered by alarms or access control events. Skydio says its data is encrypted in transit and at rest and that it aligns to SOC 2, ISO 27001 and NIST frameworks.

quote.text: Skydio drone programs help even the most dangerous work get done safer, smarter, and faster through remote autonomous flight.

paragraphs: LYT sells signal priority software that gives buses and emergency vehicles a green light at intersections, and it runs on the signal controllers and vehicle equipment an agency already has. The platform is described as cloud-based software billed as an operating expense, with predictable annual costs rather than a capital purchase.

For transit agencies, the platform models traffic and adjusts signal timing so that buses keep to schedule. For fire departments and for EMS and police, it preempts the signals ahead of responding vehicles as they approach an intersection.

LYT states that it maintains SOC 2 Type 2 compliance and that the platform is purpose-built for public agencies. Procurement routes listed on the page include a cooperative contract in Washington, a rider contract with LA Metro, and NEORide for member agencies.

paragraphs: Lexipol sells policy manuals, training, wellness resources, performance reporting, and grant support to public safety agencies, delivered through one system. Its buyers are the people running those agencies, from fire and police chiefs to risk managers, dispatch supervisors, and city administrators. An agency can begin with a single product, such as Policy or Wellness, and add others as it goes.

The policy product is the core: state-specific manuals researched and written by policy and legal professionals, then kept current as laws and standards change. Personnel acknowledge each policy electronically, which creates an audit trail for accreditation, audits, or legal reviews. Daily Training Bulletins turn those policies into practice through short scenario-based lessons. The LexOne platform ties training assignments to policy, warns leaders when licenses or credentials are about to expire, and tracks the data agencies need for reporting. Online courses carry accreditation from organizations such as IADLEST, POST, and CAPCE.

Lexipol was created in 2003 by two attorneys who were also former law enforcement officers. Co-founder Gordon Graham still records a weekly two-minute video tip for public safety and local government personnel. The company says its wellness product alone supports more than 1,000 agencies across the U.S. and Canada. Among the chiefs quoted on the site, Edward Delmore of the Gulf Shores (AL) Police Department compares a subscription to having another full-time administrator assigned to policy.

paragraphs: First Due sells cloud software that fire and EMS agencies use to run records and daily operations in one place. The suite pulls incident reporting, prevention, pre-incident planning, scheduling, assets, hydrants, training and mobile response behind a single login.

Incident documentation is built around the national fire reporting standard, with dynamic forms and error checking at submission. The patient care record is written to the NEMSIS data standard. It reads from cardiac monitors so crews do not key the same values twice. Pre-incident plans hold hazardous materials detail down to chemical location and quantity. Those plans can layer in GIS data through an Esri partnership.

The site describes CAL FIRE moving from a December decision to a July go-live. A county fire department is described using it to coordinate inspections and share preplan information with response crews. The company claims it accounts for nearly half of all NERIS submissions nationwide.

paragraphs: Motorola Solutions builds and connects technologies to protect people, property and places, supporting the collaboration between public safety agencies and enterprises. Its public safety lineup includes APX portable and mobile radios and ASTRO radio systems. On the command center side it sells NG911 call routing and call handling and Computer-Aided Dispatch. The company also designs video security and access control systems.

For police users the APX NEXT smart radio comes in single-band and multi-band configurations. The APX 8500 all-band mobile radio adds interoperability, Wi-Fi connectivity and Bluetooth in the vehicle. Vehicle routers keep first responders connected to broadband so they can reach real-time intelligence on the road. Its broadband products can run on FirstNET or on commercial carrier LTE networks. Managed, support and professional services are sold alongside to keep those systems secure and current.

Customer stories on the site include the Ouachita Parish Sheriff's Office, Peel Police, Nampa PD and York Regional Police, which serves 1.2 million residents. Hutto Independent School District uses the VB400 body camera to capture evidence in its schools. The home page announces the completed acquisition of D-Fend Solutions, which the company describes as a counter-drone technology firm.

paragraphs: ZOLL makes medical devices, software and related services for patients with serious cardiopulmonary and respiratory conditions. Its buyers include hospitals and other healthcare organizations, emergency medical services and militaries.

One part of the catalog covers acute cardiac care, from sudden cardiac death protection to heart failure management and care after a heart attack. Another covers diagnostics meant to widen access to sleep apnea testing. There is also ventilation technology for patients from neonates to adults. The Zenix monitor/defibrillator is offered for EMS and hospital use. The history page records the launch of RescueNet, described as an EMS information management system covering patient care, operational efficiency and agency compliance. A subsidiary was later renamed ZOLL Data Systems to better reflect the EMS market.

The company traces its origins to Dr. Paul Zoll, a physician who co-founded it in 1980. The history page lists the co-founders as Dr. Zoll, Leigh Stein and Thomas Claflin. Its policy for interactions with health care professionals is based on the Advanced Medical Technology Association Code of Ethics. The company also certifies a compliance program satisfying the requirements of the California Health and Safety Code. Under the Sunshine Act it tracks payments and other transfers of value and reports them annually.

paragraphs: Safety Vision designs and delivers mobile video surveillance and fleet safety systems for organizations that run vehicles. The company says it designs, builds, installs and maintains solutions for virtually any mobile video surveillance application. Hardware spans recorders, interior and exterior cameras, monitors, sensors, battery backups and portable camera kits, alongside software for managing and viewing video.

The site groups the work by industry, listing student transportation, mass transit, public safety and commercial trucking. School districts get a platform meant to increase student safety both on and off the bus, and transit fleets get equipment protecting drivers, passengers and assets. For public safety, the pages say fire, EMS and law enforcement fleets use the mobile surveillance products, and commercial vehicle customers use them to protect trucks, drivers and assets.

Software includes SafetyNET 5, a video management system the company developed, and SafeDrive AI 2, a windshield camera and recorder combining driver assistance with driver behavior monitoring. A plugin for Milestone XProtect lets on-prem and mobile video surveillance be monitored in one place. The homepage states adherence to National Defense Authorization Act requirements in procurement and membership in the AWS Partner Network.

quote.text: SMARTER SOLUTIONS SUPPORT BETTER DECISIONS.

provenance.quote: Safety Vision designs and delivers AI-powered mobile video surveillance and fleet safety solutions that help fleet managers operate safely and efficiently.
We design, build, install and maintain solutions for virtually any mobile video surveillance application.
State-of-the-art sensors. Reliable battery backups. Safety Vision has everything you need to outfit your fleet.
Safety Vision has wide-ranging expertise in every application using mobile video surveillance solutions, from public sector to private business and beyond.
Our intelligent, expandable solutions allow for a single, integrated platform to increase student safety both on and off the bus.
Whether fire, EMS or law enforcement, first responders rely on our mobile surveillance solutions to help perform their duties safely.
SafeDrive AI 2 is an intelligent windshield Camera/ DVR that integrates the functions of an advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) and driver behavior monitoring into a single powerful solution.

paragraphs: GeoCivix sells cloud-based software that cities, counties and municipalities use to run permitting, licensing, inspections, plan review and citizen services from one system. The pitch is a replacement for paper-based workflows with digital applications, automated routing, electronic plan review, mobile inspections and online payments.

Applicants use a government portal open around the clock, where they manage their projects and pay fees without calling or coming into the office. Staff mark up documents and let the system automate routing. Notifications and comment letters go back out to applicants as reviews move along. Inspectors work from a tablet or smart phone in the field, taking photos, creating reports and managing workloads on site. Permits, inspections, plans, documents, notes and approvals stay organized in one place.

Staff, reviewers, inspectors, citizens and contractors all work from the same project record. An implementation team starts by collecting application forms, communication templates, fee formulas and document workflows for configuration. The company says many agencies launch initial workflows in as little as 6 weeks, with full deployment typically completed within a few months. Every subscription is said to include unlimited technical support for all users. before.name: First Due
before.description: Cloud fire department suite: pre-incident planning, RMS, scheduling, and response - exhibited at IAFC FRI 2026, FDIC International 2026

paragraphs: First Due sells cloud software that fire and EMS agencies use to run records and daily operations in one place. The suite pulls incident reporting, prevention, pre-incident planning, scheduling, assets, hydrants, training and mobile response behind a single login.

Incident documentation is built around the national fire reporting standard, with dynamic forms and error checking at submission. The patient care record is written to the NEMSIS data standard. It reads from cardiac monitors so crews do not key the same values twice. Pre-incident plans hold hazardous materials detail down to chemical location and quantity. Those plans can layer in GIS data through an Esri partnership.

The site describes CAL FIRE moving from a December decision to a July go-live. A county fire department is described using it to coordinate inspections and share preplan information with response crews. The company claims it accounts for nearly half of all NERIS submissions nationwide.

quote.text: Born in the cloud and built to run your entire operation in one place.

provenance.quote: Born in the cloud and built to run your entire operation in one place.

First Due is NEMSIS Data Collect v3.4 and 3.5 compliant

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "© AT&T Intellectual Property. All rights reserved. FirstNet and the FirstNet logo are registered trademarks and service marks of the First Responder Network Authority." Fetched https://www.firstnet.com. The entity question in the CAUTION resolves cleanly: the footer copyright is AT&T's ('© AT&T Intellectual Property'), while the FirstNet marks are acknowledged as belonging to the First Responder Network Authority — i.e. this domain is the AT&T-operated commercial service, which is exactly the board entity 'FirstNet, Built with AT&T'. I confirmed the split by also fetching the federal side: firstnetauthority.gov states 'The First Responder Network Authority is an independent agency within the U.S. Department of Commerce's National Telecommunications and Information Administration' and sends users elsewhere for service with 'Access my FirstNet account (FirstNet.com).' So .gov is the agency, .com is the AT&T service. On rule 3: firstnet.com is NOT the parent's corporate domain (that is att.com) — it is the product's own dedicated domain with its own branding, plans and support, so it is acceptable. FLAG for the board operator, though: FirstNet does not recruit as a separate employer. Sales roles on this product are posted as AT&T requisitions, so a scraper pointed at firstnet.com will like

paragraphs: FirstNet is a wireless network built with and for the public safety community. Agencies can buy service for their teams. Individual public service professionals who pay for their own service can sign up too.

Traffic rides Band 14, described as a separate lane for time on duty or on call. Calls, texts and data always receive First Priority on the network. Phones, tablets and other hardware are certified for FirstNet before they are sold on it. Cell boosters, routers and repeaters sit alongside those handsets. So do deployables and satellite options for places where coverage falls short.

Eligibility runs across healthcare, public works, the justice system, the National Guard and more. Fire and rescue crews are offered mission-critical push-to-talk, coverage enhancements and secure apps. A dedicated team supports planned events and emergencies. The company also announced a 5G standalone core.

paragraphs: ZOLL makes medical devices, software and related services for patients with serious cardiopulmonary and respiratory conditions. Its buyers include hospitals and other healthcare organizations, emergency medical services and militaries.

One part of the catalog covers acute cardiac care, from sudden cardiac death protection to heart failure management and care after a heart attack. Another covers diagnostics meant to widen access to sleep apnea testing. There is also ventilation technology for patients from neonates to adults. The Zenix monitor/defibrillator is offered for EMS and hospital use. The history page records the launch of RescueNet, described as an EMS information management system covering patient care, operational efficiency and agency compliance. A subsidiary was later renamed ZOLL Data Systems to better reflect the EMS market.

The company traces its origins to Dr. Paul Zoll, a physician who co-founded it in 1980. The history page lists the co-founders as Dr. Zoll, Leigh Stein and Thomas Claflin. Its policy for interactions with health care professionals is based on the Advanced Medical Technology Association Code of Ethics. The company also certifies a compliance program satisfying the requirements of the California Health and Safety Code. Under the Sunshine Act it tracks payments and other transfers of value and reports them annually.

paragraphs: Tablet Command makes mobile incident command and response software for fire and EMS agencies. Commanders run an incident on a digital command board, dragging and dropping unit assignments.

The software is built on the iPad platform. A commander can tap and drag responding apparatus onto a scene, track progress against critical checklists, and time-stamp every maneuver and benchmark. Maps carry pre-plans and custom layers for hydrants, hospitals, landing zones, flood hazards and fire trails. The app is native and designed to run entirely independent of internet connectivity. It connects to CAD systems and integrates Esri GIS map layers, pre-plans, FireMapper and AVL.

The site reports over 250,000 incidents managed, covering everyday calls and multi-agency coordination. The product is also positioned as a complete replacement for mobile data terminals in the fire service. San Bernardino County Fire is named as using it in every front line response unit. A case study describes Stockton Fire Department turning to it as an MDT replacement and fire ground accountability tool.

paragraphs: First Arriving sells a real-time information platform that connects the critical systems an agency already runs. The site claims 1400+ Fire, EMS, Law Enforcement & Local Government Agencies as users. The same information shows up at the station on the big screen, in the office on a desktop, and on a tablet in the field.

The platform centralizes data from 130+ systems into one operational view. Connected sources include CAD, RMS, staffing, fleet, facilities, GIS, scheduling, training, and alerts. Alerts can be pushed with required acknowledgments so the right people act immediately. Individual user accounts and role-based views mean each member of a team sees what they need.

The law enforcement version is designed for police departments, sheriff's offices, campus safety, and agencies of all sizes. It carries things like daily shift briefings and watch commander notes. A local government version covers council meetings, facility schedules, emergency alerts, and public notices. Lobbies, public counters and reception areas are named as display locations. The company notes that its marketing division is now ResponderMAX.

paragraphs: 3AM Innovations sells FLORIAN, safety software that shows a command center where every responder and resource is while an incident is under way. The company says it was started by firefighters, and it now aims the same idea at any team that has to keep track of people in the field.

FLORIAN runs on the phone or tablet a responder already carries, sending location and movement back to the command center in real time. It reports position in three dimensions, including elevation, so command can tell where someone sits inside a structure. Licensing splits in two, with the Advanced plan positioned for teams that regularly face complicated calls. That tier adds geofencing and Mayday alerts. Groups that need to stand something up quickly can order deployable kits, which ship with devices already carrying Advanced licenses.

Beyond the fire service, the company points to campus security teams and the organizers of large events such as marathons. 3AM says it belongs to purchasing vehicles including GSA and SAVVIK, which can let a buyer skip the RFP process. It also offers support services covering setup, training and deployment.

paragraphs: Miovision sells traffic data collection tools meant to give planners the accurate, verifiable data their mobility plans depend on. It also sells detection equipment that improves signal performance by responding to real-world road user demand, from bicycles to articulated trucks. Its Opticom line clears the path for emergency fleets without re-timing entire corridors.

Portable devices capture comprehensive multimodal count data including cars, trucks, pedestrians and bikes. A newer optimization product replaces manual five-year retiming cycles with iterative, objective-based optimization that the company says cuts manual effort by up to half. Engineers compare plans side-by-side, validate against industry standards, and push updates directly to field controllers without manual data re-entry.

The company says that since 2005 it has had 2,000 customers in 68 countries and 13,000 cities, with 30 billion vehicles and 1.5 billion pedestrians counted. It lists more than 300 detection customers in North America. Detroit partnered with Miovision to upgrade over 600 intersections. In San Rafael, police and fire vehicles now receive signal priority at 53 intersections.

paragraphs: Motorola Solutions builds and connects technologies to protect people, property and places, supporting the collaboration between public safety agencies and enterprises. Its public safety lineup includes APX portable and mobile radios and ASTRO radio systems. On the command center side it sells NG911 call routing and call handling and Computer-Aided Dispatch. The company also designs video security and access control systems.

For police users the APX NEXT smart radio comes in single-band and multi-band configurations. The APX 8500 all-band mobile radio adds interoperability, Wi-Fi connectivity and Bluetooth in the vehicle. Vehicle routers keep first responders connected to broadband so they can reach real-time intelligence on the road. Its broadband products can run on FirstNET or on commercial carrier LTE networks. Managed, support and professional services are sold alongside to keep those systems secure and current.

Customer stories on the site include the Ouachita Parish Sheriff's Office, Peel Police, Nampa PD and York Regional Police, which serves 1.2 million residents. Hutto Independent School District uses the VB400 body camera to capture evidence in its schools. The home page announces the completed acquisition of D-Fend Solutions, which the company describes as a counter-drone technology firm.

paragraphs: LION Group sells fire training equipment and facilities, and its own pages describe it as the largest provider of that equipment for first responders. The training catalogue runs from live fire props such as the Vehicle Fire Training Prop and the Dumpster Fire Training Prop to digital systems and smoke generators. Protective equipment covers turnout gear, helmets, hoods, gloves, boots and coveralls, with hoods sold under the RedZone name.

Uniforms are listed as Fire Uniforms, Law Enforcement Uniforms and EMS Uniforms. Gear care is sold as TotalCare, covering cleaning, inspection and repair, and the pages also list a PPE rental program. A supply chain arm is named as LVI Military Logistics.

On who buys, the site says LION is big enough to deliver on the largest fire department contracts. The same sentence names every emergency responder and firefighter that uses the equipment. Buyers are pointed to a sales rep by state, and the page also lists a dealer finder and an online shop.

paragraphs: Esri builds ArcGIS, its geographic information system software for mapping and spatial analysis. The company describes itself as the global market leader in GIS software, location intelligence, and mapping. Its stated audience is business, government, and society.

ArcGIS is presented as enterprise technology that integrates and connects data through the context of geography. The premise is that hidden patterns, trends, and relationships emerge once data is visualized and analyzed on a map. Beyond maps and analysis, the company says its technology speeds data sharing and collaboration. For agencies that want to keep everything in house, there is a self-hosted edition for mapping, analytics, and data management.

Esri says it has supported customers with geographic science and geospatial analytics since 1969. Officials working in public safety, transportation, infrastructure, health and human services, and other fields use the technology to support high-level decisions. At the local level, the company says community leaders apply it to economic development, public works, and urban planning. Published stories include the US Census Bureau modernizing its entire census process with GIS.

before.description: Safety Cloud digital alerting for DOT, fire and public works fleets - exhibited at IAFC FRI 2026, ITS America 2026, FDIC International 2026
before.source: competitor sweep; IAFC FRI 2026; ITS America 2026; FDIC International 2026

paragraphs: HAAS Alert sells a collision prevention service that sends real-time digital alerts warning drivers about nearby emergency vehicles and roadway hazards. Its customers are fleets that work at the roadside, including tow trucks, utility vehicles, waste management trucks, school buses and snowplows.

The system is wired to a vehicle's warning light bar or master switch, so alerting begins when crews turn on their lights and stops when they turn them off. Motorists install nothing, because alerts are broadcast directly to the navigation platforms they already use. Fleets can activate the service through three primary methods, depending on their existing setup. The company says drivers get up to 30 seconds of advance warning to slow down and move over.

The company traces its start to 2015, when co-founder and CEO Cory Hohs was almost struck by an ambulance on the road. He co-founded the business with Noah Levens and Jigar Patel. Its timeline notes that the United States Department of Homeland Security awarded $1.1 million toward development for digital alerting. It also states that digital alerting was codified and funded in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

before.name: ImageTrend
before.description: Incident records and ePCR data platform for EMS and fire agencies - exhibited at IAFC FRI 2026, FDIC International 2026
before.source: direct add; IAFC FRI 2026; FDIC International 2026

paragraphs: ImageTrend sells software that fire departments, EMS agencies, and hospitals run their emergency response operations on. Its core product is ePCR software built for how medics actually work, with AI-assisted documentation, configurable workflows, and real-time intelligence for agencies at any scale.

The platform connects scheduling, documentation, compliance, unified analytics, operational readiness, and hospital data exchange in one system. NEMSIS, NERIS, NTDB, and TQIP compliance is built into every workflow, with software filling and validating fields while staff review and confirm before submission. A scheduling product, ImageTrend Slate, addresses the demands of EMS, fire departments, and other critical services. It manages time-off requests, shift trades, and employee availability. Separate pre-plan software digitizes floor plans, hazard locations, water supply points, and utility shutoffs so responders have instant access to tactical data on scene.

The company reports 9,000 agencies, 43 state repositories, and more than a billion records processed. It says its sales engineering team is entirely former fire and EMS. It cites 24/7 US-based support and a 96.5% satisfaction rate, backed by 25 years in the field.

quote.text: Other vendors build software and ask you to fit your operation around it.

paragraphs: Lexipol sells policy manuals, training, wellness resources, performance reporting, and grant support to public safety agencies, delivered through one system. Its buyers are the people running those agencies, from fire and police chiefs to risk managers, dispatch supervisors, and city administrators. An agency can begin with a single product, such as Policy or Wellness, and add others as it goes.

The policy product is the core: state-specific manuals researched and written by policy and legal professionals, then kept current as laws and standards change. Personnel acknowledge each policy electronically, which creates an audit trail for accreditation, audits, or legal reviews. Daily Training Bulletins turn those policies into practice through short scenario-based lessons. The LexOne platform ties training assignments to policy, warns leaders when licenses or credentials are about to expire, and tracks the data agencies need for reporting. Online courses carry accreditation from organizations such as IADLEST, POST, and CAPCE.

Lexipol was created in 2003 by two attorneys who were also former law enforcement officers. Co-founder Gordon Graham still records a weekly two-minute video tip for public safety and local government personnel. The company says its wellness product alone supports more than 1,000 agencies across the U.S. and Canada. Among the chiefs quoted on the site, Edward Delmore of the Gulf Shores (AL) Police Department compares a subscription to having another full-time administrator assigned to policy.

quote.text: We help public safety agencies and municipalities operate at the highest standards.

paragraphs: Versaterm sells software to public safety agencies, built around a CAD system so that dispatch and the field work from the same real-time information. Records are the other core piece, and Versaterm says a modern RMS cuts manual effort and keeps information available from patrol through command.

Named products for community communication include Versaterm CommunityConnect, Versaterm CommunityReport, Versaterm CallTriage, and Versaterm Public Portal. Versaterm IAPro and Versaterm BlueTeam cover professional standards work, alongside professional standards training. Two further named products are Versaterm Mindbase and Versaterm EIPro.

DroneSense by Versaterm handles drone operations, and Glendale Police uses Versaterm DroneSense flight management software with the SafeSky traffic awareness app. The company says it has worked with agencies for over 47 years. The Sumner County Sheriff's Office won first place in the 2026 Versaterm Innovation Awards for its use of technology and data in its school resource officer division.

quote.text: Protecting communities requires clarity before action, accountability after and care throughout every response, supported by responsible innovation.

before.name: Handtevy
before.description: Pediatric emergency dosing system and app for EMS agencies

paragraphs: Handtevy sells clinical workflow software for emergency medicine, pairing precision dosing and protocol access for clinicians with control and reporting for the administrators who oversee them. The buyers are agencies and hospitals looking to raise their standard of emergency care.

Handtevy Mobile puts precision dosing, real-time protocols, and clinical decision support directly in clinicians' hands. Weight-based calculations are cross-checked against clinical thresholds and customized to local protocols. An admin portal lets administrators manage pharmacology, protocols, order sets, and checklists across an organization and control exactly what clinicians see at the point of care. The software connects directly with ePCR and EHR platforms, which the company says involves no PHI exposure and no IT infrastructure.

The company says it is used by more than 200,000 clinicians in all 50 states. Pediatric Emergency Standards, Inc. has operated under the name Handtevy since 2010, offering evidence-based software to healthcare providers domestically and internationally. Its founder, Dr. Peter Antevy, is a practicing pediatric emergency medicine physician and EMS Medical Director. The company started in pediatrics and now describes its goal as improving emergency care for adults as well.

quote.text: Handtevy is a preeminent pediatric system of care relied on by clinicians in the emergency medical field worldwide.

before.description: Marketplace for used fire trucks and public safety equipment: appraisals, payments, financing ($13.5M raised, YC) - exhibited at FDIC International 2026

paragraphs: Garage runs an online marketplace for specialized vehicles and equipment in the United States. Much of the inventory is fire apparatus, sorted into categories such as rescue trucks and squads. Other browsing categories include brush trucks and mini pumpers. Roll offs and hooklifts get a category of their own as well.

Each listing is headed by the year, manufacturer and body style of the truck. Under that heading, the listing states mileage, water tank capacity and pump rating. Mileage varies widely, with some pumpers listed past 100,000 miles. Aerial listings add ladder height to those figures.

The catalog reaches past the fire service into ambulances of several body types. Refuse collection trucks are listed too, including automated side loaders. So are hydro excavation and sewer trucks. Septic trucks appear in the same catalog.

before.description: Fire helmets and thermal imaging cameras for fire departments - exhibited at FDIC International 2026

paragraphs: Bullard makes protective equipment worn on the job: hard hats, face shields, respirators, fire helmets and thermal imaging cameras. Fire departments are among the buyers, taking helmets for protection and thermal imagers as a second set of eyes in smoke.

The respiratory line serves healthcare, pharmaceutical and industrial settings where workers face pathogens, particulates, mist, vapors and sprays. Abrasive blasting gets its own complete systems, bundling a helmet with airline hose, climate control and a carbon monoxide monitor. Buyers configure gear on the site and get a suggested retail price to take to a distributor.

The company traces its line of work back to designing the first hard hat in 1919, and has been in blasting equipment for over half a century. It sells through channel partners around the world rather than direct, and lists its address in Cynthiana, Kentucky.

before.source: APTA 2026; NSA 2026; CTAA EXPO 2026; NAPT Summit 2026; SWANA WASTECON 2025; FDIC International 2026
before.buyer: School districts are the largest named segment (700+ districts, 30M+ bus route miles); also mass transit agencies (25M+ commuters), EMS/emergency services, and commercial trucking

paragraphs: Safety Vision designs and delivers mobile video surveillance and fleet safety systems for organizations that run vehicles. The company says it designs, builds, installs and maintains solutions for virtually any mobile video surveillance application. Hardware spans recorders, interior and exterior cameras, monitors, sensors, battery backups and portable camera kits, alongside software for managing and viewing video.

The site groups the work by industry, listing student transportation, mass transit, public safety and commercial trucking. School districts get a platform meant to increase student safety both on and off the bus, and transit fleets get equipment protecting drivers, passengers and assets. For public safety, the pages say fire, EMS and law enforcement fleets use the mobile surveillance products, and commercial vehicle customers use them to protect trucks, drivers and assets.

Software includes SafetyNET 5, a video management system the company developed, and SafeDrive AI 2, a windshield camera and recorder combining driver assistance with driver behavior monitoring. A plugin for Milestone XProtect lets on-prem and mobile video surveillance be monitored in one place. The homepage states adherence to National Defense Authorization Act requirements in procurement and membership in the AWS Partner Network.

quote.text: SMARTER SOLUTIONS SUPPORT BETTER DECISIONS.

provenance.quote: Safety Vision designs and delivers AI-powered mobile video surveillance and fleet safety solutions that help fleet managers operate safely and efficiently.

paragraphs: Derq builds intelligent transportation systems for safer roads. It sells to agencies, helping them improve safety and optimize traffic flow for all road users.

The platform detects, tracks, classifies, and predicts road user behavior in real time, and the company says it does so accurately in all weather and lighting conditions. It is compatible with a wide range of sensors, including video detection, CCTV and radar, as well as traffic controllers and V2X technologies. Edge-based traffic detection covers vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists. Analytics deliver safety insights, traffic performance data, near-miss insights, and ATSPMs. V2X applications are aimed at preventing collisions between vehicles and vulnerable road users.

Derq describes itself as an MIT spinoff founded in 2016. It says its technology is live across the United States, Canada, and the GCC. The company reports more than 20 patents. It states that it is SOC 2 Type II compliant. The site also announces that Derq was named a winner of the USDOT Intersection Safety Challenge.

paragraphs: Dareesoft sells road hazard detection that rides along in vehicles already using the road network. The offering is packaged as Road Information as a Service, an all-in-one solution for road maintenance. The company describes itself as an integrated road data company.

A device in the vehicle analyzes the road and transmits hazards to a cloud platform instantly. Each detection carries a high quality image with GPS coordinates, road network, timestamps and object size. Detected hazards appear on a road monitoring dashboard for remote inspection. An API suite lets the hazard data flow into systems an agency already runs.

Dareesoft was founded in 2020. Its company timeline lists a contract for the Seoul Metropolitan Government video-based pothole detection project. The same timeline records a project secured with Brazoria County, Texas. Another entry lists a project contract signed with New York City for speed signage. It also lists a Series B raise of KRW 4 billion.

paragraphs: GoodVision sells traffic analysis software to transportation professionals, who use it to collect, analyze and act on traffic data taken from video footage or live camera streams. Its main platform, Video Insights, extracts data from videos in place of manual collection and uses AI to analyze traffic and automate model calibration.

A second product works on live feeds rather than uploads, analysing camera streams on the fly and passing traffic data to third-party systems such as traffic management systems and controllers. The incident detection module recognises user-defined traffic events, flags them and reports them to traffic management centre controllers. At intersections and roundabouts it counts volumes and derives parameters such as speed, gaps between vehicles, dwell time and passage time. Finished reports can be edited, regenerated and exported in Excel, CSV or custom formats.

The company describes the same monitoring applied to bridges and tunnels, where the goal is to prevent congestion and catch accidents early. Alongside direct sales, GoodVision runs a partner program and says it is seeking global distribution and service partners.

paragraphs: Wavetronix makes radar sensors that detect the presence of vehicles at the stop bar. The buyers are traffic agencies, and the collected data can be shared among several of them. That data feeds uses such as trip times and congestion alerts.

One system is a multi-approach stop bar detector designed for smaller intersections. It covers four approaches of three lanes or less per approach. The flagship stop bar detector sees both moving and stopped vehicles. A safety product tracks vehicles in the dilemma zone out to 600 feet. An extended range version protects large trucks and buses out to 900 feet. A cabinet device supplies power and communication for two to six sensors. A newer add-on analyzes split failures and turning movement counts and recommends updated max green times.

The company says it opened in 2000. All sensors are made at its headquarters in Springville, Utah. It states that it supports and complies with the Build America Buy America Act. It also says it is driven to succeed for customers, not for investors or shareholders.

paragraphs: StreetLight sells transportation analytics built on a big data platform rather than on field counts. The platform covers roadway volumes, transportation modeling, congestion management and safety studies, with AADT and origin-destination metrics. Delivery runs three ways: self-serve software, bulk data through an API, and custom services from a data science team.

Products are grouped by industry, and the groupings named on the site are government, business, consultants and academics. paragraphs: Esri builds ArcGIS, its geographic information system software for mapping and spatial analysis. The company describes itself as the global market leader in GIS software, location intelligence, and mapping. Its stated audience is business, government, and society.

ArcGIS is presented as enterprise technology that integrates and connects data through the context of geography. The premise is that hidden patterns, trends, and relationships emerge once data is visualized and analyzed on a map. Beyond maps and analysis, the company says its technology speeds data sharing and collaboration. For agencies that want to keep everything in house, there is a self-hosted edition for mapping, analytics, and data management.

Esri says it has supported customers with geographic science and geospatial analytics since 1969. Officials working in public safety, transportation, infrastructure, health and human services, and other fields use the technology to support high-level decisions. At the local level, the company says community leaders apply it to economic development, public works, and urban planning. Published stories include the US Census Bureau modernizing its entire census process with GIS.

paragraphs: Quarterhill designs, develops, and deploys technology systems for the intelligent transportation systems industry, with a presence throughout North America and Europe. Its tolling work covers toll collection, and its safety and enforcement work covers commercial vehicle enforcement, freight compliance, and active transportation management. Multi modal solutions cover container tracking and port planning, border crossings, and axle-load and track monitoring on rail lines and highway corridors.

Rail products built on Sensor Line fiber optic sensors cover speed measurement, weigh in motion, flat wheel detection, track bed analysis, axle and wagon counting, and vibration analysis. These sensors are used for predictive maintenance and for detecting changes to track and rolling stock.

Customers named on the site include government agencies, toll operators, and private sectors, along with Departments of Transportation, logistics providers, local governments, and law enforcement agencies. Enforcement agencies use the commercial vehicle inspection technologies in over 2000 lanes worldwide to prevent weigh station congestion. The company handles over 2 billion toll transactions each year for toll authorities in the United States.

paragraphs: Cyclomedia sells geospatial data built from street-level imagery, lidar point clouds, and aerial data covering public space. Public authorities are a core market, using it to manage streets, buildings, and public assets. Utility and energy providers use it to plan, inspect, and manage their networks.

Street Smart, the company's viewer, brings 360 degree imagery, lidar, and map layers into one browser-based workspace. From the desk, users measure distances along facades, pavements, and openings. Automated analysis detects pavement defects, surface types, and deterioration in high-resolution imagery. Property valuation is another stated use, supported by current visual evidence and measurements. Open integrations and APIs connect the data to existing GIS and asset management systems.

The company says it has worked in geospatial capture and visualisation for more than 40 years with public authorities across Europe and beyond. Specialised capture vehicles survey cities and regions throughout the year. Routes are coordinated with local authorities to limit disruption. before.name: B2Gnow
before.description: Supplier diversity and DBE compliance tracking SaaS for states, cities, airports, and transit - exhibited at NIGP 2026

paragraphs: B2Gnow sells compliance software to public agencies and the contractors on their projects, covering vendor programs, prevailing wage labor compliance and grant management. The company lists states, state DOTs, cities, counties, transit agencies, airports, education, general contractors and healthcare among the kinds of clients it names.

The vendor side is a cloud-based platform covering DBE, MBE, WBE and SBE compliance initiatives. Certification work runs from online applications through agency review to approval. For contract compliance, prime and subcontractor payments are collected, and subcontractors confirm payment directly, monthly or quarterly. Reporting draws on more than 400 standard system reports. A payroll line covers Davis-Bacon and Related Acts, the Service Contract Act, state prevailing wage laws and local living wage ordinances. Grant work runs through BlackCat, from applications to asset management and spend-down tracking.

The company says the software has been implemented at over 400 organizations. It claims one million users regularly access the system to register, prequalify, submit reports, manage grants and review bid solicitations. The site cites over 25 years of vendor program compliance experience. B2Gnow and eComply have joined together into one platform spanning vendor management and labor compliance. Hosting is described as fully redundant, with guaranteed availability of 99.9% and SOC 2 Type 2 certification.

paragraphs: Flock Safety sells license plate readers, video cameras, gunshot detection and response drones to law enforcement agencies, schools, businesses and neighborhoods to help them deter crime, respond to emergencies and investigate safety incidents. Its license plate recognition cameras capture plates and vehicle characteristics such as make, color and body type to generate investigative leads. Responders get an instant alert when a vehicle matches a customer-defined or NCIC hot list. Users include law enforcement agencies, businesses, neighborhoods, apartment complexes, houses of worship and schools.

Beyond plate readers, Flock sells PTZ video cameras for open areas such as parking lots, intersections and parks, and fixed cameras for buildings and city streets. A gunshot and audio detection product verifies gunfire and links each alert with nearby LPR reads and video. Flock DFR, its drone as first responder system, launches a docked drone to the coordinates of a 911 call, LPR hit or gunshot alert and streams live video to officers before they arrive. Solar-powered mobile trailers cover parking lots, retail centers and construction sites, and an optional Alert Response Service puts trained agents on live alerts.

Flock sells on an annual subscription that covers hardware, software, maintenance and support. The company has reduced its recommended default data retention from 30 days to 7 days, which it says applies to new law enforcement customers. Customers control their data and how it is shared, and every search is logged.

Private: HOAs and neighborhood associations, multifamily communities, retail and grocery (Academy Sports is named), retail banking, healthcare, hospitality, logistics, manufacturing, builders and developers, property managers and places of worship.
before.scope_note: Their customers page states the split itself: "5,000+ Law Enforcement Agencies," "6,000+ Communities" and "1,000+ Businesses." The HOA page makes the private buyer explicit — "Your HOA owns all footage and data" and "Law enforcement only gains access if your HOA opts in" — so the HOA, not a city, is the contracting party there. Our "Police" category captures their largest and most visible segment and is fair, but be aware roughly half their published industry pages are commercial; if the board ever filters on "government-only vendors," Flock should not be in that bucket.

before.name: Miovision
before.description: Traffic data collection and smart intersection technology - exhibited at IAFC FRI 2026, APTA 2026, FDIC International 2026, FDIC International 2027
before.source: APTA 2026; IAFC FRI 2026; FDIC International 2026; FDIC International 2027

paragraphs: Miovision sells traffic data collection tools meant to give planners the accurate, verifiable data their mobility plans depend on. It also sells detection equipment that improves signal performance by responding to real-world road user demand, from bicycles to articulated trucks. Its Opticom line clears the path for emergency fleets without re-timing entire corridors.

Portable devices capture comprehensive multimodal count data including cars, trucks, pedestrians and bikes. A newer optimization product replaces manual five-year retiming cycles with iterative, objective-based optimization that the company says cuts manual effort by up to half. Engineers compare plans side-by-side, validate against industry standards, and push updates directly to field controllers without manual data re-entry.

The company says that since 2005 it has had 2,000 customers in 68 countries and 13,000 cities, with 30 billion vehicles and 1.5 billion pedestrians counted. It lists more than 300 detection customers in North America. Detroit partnered with Miovision to upgrade over 600 intersections. In San Rafael, police and fire vehicles now receive signal priority at 53 intersections.

paragraphs: ESO makes documentation and records software for the people who respond to emergencies, starting with paramedics writing up a call. Fire departments are a second audience, where the pitch is management insight into performance and readiness.

The products are framed as one ecosystem, with patient records shared securely with prehospital partners in real time. Hospitals get a version aimed past compliance reporting, toward spotting risk and emerging trends. Product news on the home page includes Agency Forms for the company's EHR.

A fire and emergency services analyst is among the customers quoted on the home page. ESO says the data at the center of that ecosystem fuels research that shapes clinical protocols and public policy. The about page points to published research papers that feature ESO data. It also publishes indices, among them a 2026 ESO Fire Service Index.

before.name: PSTrax
before.description: Cloud checklist and compliance management: vehicle checks, SCBA, PPE, and narcotics for 1,400+ agencies - exhibited at IAFC FRI 2026, FDIC International 2026

paragraphs: PSTrax sells digital inventory and asset management software built for first responders. The system tracks inspections of vehicles, stations, equipment, supplies, controlled substances and blood products.

Rather than handing over a toolkit, the company builds and implements each system for the department and to that department's specs. Systems are meant to be ready to roll out in a matter of weeks. Ongoing support for changes is unlimited and comes at no extra cost. A one-year money back guarantee is offered to customers.

PSTrax, short for Public Safety Tracking Systems, was founded by Scott Bergeron and Cliff Long in 2009. It is headquartered in Littleton, Colorado, with 22 full-time employees. The company says it serves more than 1,000 organizations worldwide. That count includes more than 850 Fire-EMS agencies across the United States, Canada and Australia. It is privately held and says it answers to customers rather than to VC firms or shareholders. It reports a 98.5% customer retention rate.

quote.text: Creating a world where every first responder knows with certainty that their equipment, assets, and inventories are ready for the next call.

Rather than handing over a toolkit, the company builds and implements each system for the department and to that department's specs. Systems are meant to be ready to roll out in a matter of weeks. Ongoing support for changes is unlimited and comes at no extra cost. A one-year money back guarantee is offered to customers.

PSTrax, short for Public Safety Tracking Systems, was founded by Scott Bergeron and Cliff Long in 2009. It is headquartered in Littleton, Colorado, with 22 full-time employees. The company says it serves more than 1,000 organizations worldwide. That count includes more than 850 Fire-EMS agencies across the United States, Canada and Australia. It is privately held and says it answers to customers rather than to VC firms or shareholders. It reports a 98.5% customer retention rate.

paragraphs: Esri builds ArcGIS, its geographic information system software for mapping and spatial analysis. The company describes itself as the global market leader in GIS software, location intelligence, and mapping. Its stated audience is business, government, and society.

ArcGIS is presented as enterprise technology that integrates and connects data through the context of geography. The premise is that hidden patterns, trends, and relationships emerge once data is visualized and analyzed on a map. Beyond maps and analysis, the company says its technology speeds data sharing and collaboration. For agencies that want to keep everything in house, there is a self-hosted edition for mapping, analytics, and data management.

Esri says it has supported customers with geographic science and geospatial analytics since 1969. Officials working in public safety, transportation, infrastructure, health and human services, and other fields use the technology to support high-level decisions. At the local level, the company says community leaders apply it to economic development, public works, and urban planning. Published stories include the US Census Bureau modernizing its entire census process with GIS.

paragraphs: EagleView sells aerial imagery and property data drawn from an archive the company puts at more than 3.5 billion high-resolution images. Public agencies are one audience, with the imagery aimed at tax assessment, zoning enforcement, emergency response and infrastructure planning.

The subscription imagery product refreshes annually at 2-inch resolution, with an option to upgrade. The company says its 1-inch imagery carries nine times more detail than 3-inch imagery. Captures include straight-down orthogonal views for mapping and measurement and angled oblique views of building sides. A separate archive holds more than 25 years of imagery covering 96 percent of the United States population. New content is added daily, with annual refreshes across metro areas and high-growth regions. Customers view imagery in a browser tool or pull it through API connections into GIS, CAD, CAMA or analytics systems.
The site states that 20 of the top 20 insurers rely on the company. Governments, insurers, utilities, AEC firms and environmental professionals are named as users of the imagery archive.

paragraphs: Survalent sells control room software to utilities, bringing SCADA, outage management and distribution management into one system. The company describes its buyers as electric, water and wastewater, oil and gas, renewable energy and transit utilities around the world. It argues that running a distribution network well is hard without a modern, centralized supervisory control and data acquisition system.

One network model and one database sit under every application, so a change made once carries across the platform. Operators work from real-time equipment status, metering data, alarming and control, with the aim of catching problems before outages start. A utility can start with a limited set of feeders, substations and applications and add more over time. A metering interface pulls readings from the AMI system using the MultiSpeak protocol, and a lightning interface fetches strike data and filters it by the utility's area of interest.

MultiSpeak itself is described as an initiative for rural electric co-ops and municipal utilities. The site says more than 700 utilities worldwide use its SCADA product. It reports 800+ customers around the world and 97.6% customer retention. The company also says it puts 20.3% of revenue into research and development.

paragraphs: Paladin autonomously deploys drones to emergency incidents so that aerial views reach responders before the first unit arrives. A drone launches automatically from the department's dock as soon as an incident is reported. The company states that responders get eyes on scene in under 90 seconds. The platform is meant for departments regardless of city size and integrates with dispatch workflows.

Paladin supplies the drone, the software, the data management platform and the FAA waivers a department needs to operate legally. Its drone for emergency response, the Knighthawk, is made in the United States. The company describes that drone as NDAA approved and autonomous. A partnership with T-Mobile extends how far the drones can travel.

Ferguson PD in Missouri implemented a Drone-as-First-Responder program with Paladin to improve response times and increase situational awareness. Forest Park PD in Georgia deployed the system for aerial visibility across incidents. Murrells Inlet FD in South Carolina uses it for fire, EMS and search operations. Elizabeth PD in New Jersey scaled from a single drone to a fully staffed 24/7 operation. Divy Shrivastava founded the company and has led it since 2018.

paragraphs: RapidSOS connects public safety agencies, enterprises and large numbers of consumer and corporate devices so emergency information reaches responders. The company states it partners with over 250 enterprise companies and 23,500 public safety agencies.

The premise is that connected systems can share information with responders even before a 911 call is placed. One police department describes adopting a module built around AI-powered live text translation, transcription and call summarization. In an Atlanta deployment, translation covered over 37 languages by voice and over 200 by text. Another center is described using Harmony AI to handle non-emergency calls.

The homepage says agencies and enterprises on the network safeguard over 99% of the country. Published case studies sort customers into categories such as connected vehicles and telematics. One partner statement on the site is attributed to a VP of Safety at Norfolk Southern. A documented problem it addresses is waiting up to ten minutes for a translator on a 911 call.

before.name: Econolite
before.description: Traffic signal controllers, cabinets, and intersection management systems

paragraphs: Econolite sells traffic management equipment and services to transportation agencies responsible for roadway efficiency. The catalog includes traffic control cabinets in standard configurations and to unique specifications. It sells traffic signal controllers for intersection management. Detection sensors cover vehicles, bicycles and pedestrians. The company is also a licensed electrical contractor doing traffic signal and ITS maintenance and repair.

Its cabinet designs draw on features of Caltrans, NEMA and ITS cabinets. The Advanced Traffic Control Cabinet uses high-speed serial communications. Its standard configuration allows up to 32 signal outputs and 120 detection inputs. A separate line covers NEMA TS1 and TS2 cabinets built for traffic applications. Battery backup keeps signals operating during a power disruption.

Agencies can book an on-site session with the company to review cabinet performance and specifications. Recent site news names a distributor for the Northwest United States. It also reports European Union certification for a radar detection product. Another item describes adaptive traffic control in Hamburg with Umovity and PTV Group.

before.name: Handtevy
before.description: Pediatric emergency dosing system and app for EMS agencies - exhibited at FDIC International 2027

paragraphs: Handtevy sells clinical workflow software for emergency medicine, pairing precision dosing and protocol access for clinicians with control and reporting for the administrators who oversee them. The buyers are agencies and hospitals looking to raise their standard of emergency care.

Handtevy Mobile puts precision dosing, real-time protocols, and clinical decision support directly in clinicians' hands. Weight-based calculations are cross-checked against clinical thresholds and customized to local protocols. An admin portal lets administrators manage pharmacology, protocols, order sets, and checklists across an organization and control exactly what clinicians see at the point of care. The software connects directly with ePCR and EHR platforms, which the company says involves no PHI exposure and no IT infrastructure.

The company says it is used by more than 200,000 clinicians in all 50 states. Pediatric Emergency Standards, Inc. has operated under the name Handtevy since 2010, offering evidence-based software to healthcare providers domestically and internationally. Its founder, Dr. Peter Antevy, is a practicing pediatric emergency medicine physician and EMS Medical Director. The company started in pediatrics and now describes its goal as improving emergency care for adults as well.

paragraphs: ICC Innovation is the arm of the International Code Council that packages digital tools and software as a service applications for communities. It is offered as an end-to-end suite backed by expert resources.

The lineup includes digital codification tools meant to support safety, compliance and efficiency. A flexible online code experience is offered to raise transparency and efficiency. Content management and process automation route work, requests and notifications so employees and residents can do business from anywhere. Permitting moves online, covering applications, inspection scheduling and application review. Electronic plan review is presented as a secure way to speed up the permit application process.

Training and certification options earn CEUs, LUs or PDHs toward International Code Council certification renewal. The Code Council is steered by a board that meets several times a year to provide oversight and strategic direction. The organization states its mission as building safety. Staff leaders run daily operations for their areas across the family of companies. One address it lists is in Washington, DC.

before.name: Accela
before.description: Permitting, licensing, and code enforcement platform for state and local government - exhibited at NLC City Summit 2026, ICMA 2026, NRPA 2026, ICC 2026
before.source: ICMA 2025; NRPA 2026; ICMA 2026; NLC City Summit 2026; ICC 2026

paragraphs: Accela sells software that government agencies use to run permitting, licensing, and asset management from a single system. Its applications are built for individual government service workflows and can operate together or be deployed only where an agency needs them.

For building departments, intake, plan review, inspections, and permit issuance sit in one workflow rather than in separate disconnected steps. Reviewers from different departments work the same record at once, with annotations and approvals tracked as they happen. Planning teams get the same shared review model, plus automated public notice generation, hearing schedules, and agency notifications. Applicants can see where a case stands and receive consolidated feedback from every reviewing department.

The company says it has thirty years of government expertise built into the product. Testimonials on the site are attributed to municipal staff, including a chief building official in McAllen, Texas. Residents and businesses who encounter Accela through a local agency are directed to that agency rather than to the company.

quote.text: The end-to-end platform for permitting, licensing, asset management and more. Built for high performing agencies.

before.name: Archistar
before.description: AI planning and building code assessment tools sold to councils and cities - exhibited at ICMA 2026, Smart Cities Connect 2026, ICC 2026
before.source: competitor sweep; ICMA 2026; Smart Cities Connect 2026; ICC 2026

paragraphs: Archistar sells AI plan review software to local governments, with a product called AI PreCheck that speeds building code and zoning compliance checks so permits can be issued faster. The same platform is offered to developers, architects and certifiers, who can check compliance before submitting to a municipality or council.

Submitters drag and drop design files onto the platform, which accepts PDF, CAD or BIM formats and reviews them in 2D or 3D. The software then evaluates each submission against the city's local codes and regulations. It is built on generative AI, computer vision and machine learning. Applicants receive standardized reports. For municipalities and councils with particular zoning, planning and compliance requirements, tailored and white-labeled versions are offered.

The company says Archistar was founded by Dr. Benjamin Coorey in 2010 and began life as an education portal. It grew from a university research project into a platform that could read planning rules, run feasibility tests and generate compliant designs in minutes. The site states that Archistar powers digital planning for over 30 cities and governments across Australia, Canada and the United States. Among the municipalities it names supporting are LA County, the City of Los Angeles, the City of Austin and the City of New York. Offices are listed across Los Angeles, Vancouver and Sydney.

quote.text: What once took weeks of back-and-forth can now happen in seconds.
