paragraphs: Konveio sells an engagement platform built around planning documents and the full plan lifecycle. The platform is split into an Engagement Hub for public input and a Plan Hub that publishes a Plan Library. Organizations upload materials they already have and take comments on them in place. The company dates its inception to 2020.

Staff can export data to CSV or download annotated PDF reports. Comments from events, letters and emails can be imported and analyzed in one place. The viewer is described as mobile-friendly, WCAG compliant, and screen-reader accessible.

Local Governments are named as an audience, from early stage outreach through implementation stages. State agencies are named for work groups and for drafting policy and legislation. Consultants are named, with plans described as fitting tight budgets or project needs. Colleges, universities and school districts are named for community outreach projects.

quote.text: Konveio's mission is to help community builders get informed buy-in for their efforts to create a better tomorrow.

paragraphs: Madison AI sells a platform that turns a government's own files and systems into an AI assistant for staff. The pages describe drafting staff reports, looking up code and zoning by parcel, researching voting history, and analyzing contracts against procurement standards. The homepage states that the product makes work easier in local government and water districts.

The site says the engine was created by Washoe County and OnStrategy. The about page names Washoe County as a co-founder and an equity partner rather than only a customer. The site names the City of Reno, Washoe County, and the Northern Nevada Regional Transportation Commission among government clients.

Deployment is described as taking about four weeks, with full deployment in less than sixty days. The homepage says the product is used by 65+ local governments and counting. A time study by the City of Reno is cited as reducing staff report production by more than 75%.

paragraphs: GovWell sells software that city and county governments use to run permitting, licensing, planning, and code enforcement work. Residents and businesses use the same system to reach services, pay, and get answers outside office hours.

Permits, plan review, and inspections are handled together in one place for staff. Licensing runs online too, with applicants filing, paying, and renewing while staff keep records and approvals on their side. Code enforcement officers track cases, schedule inspections, and follow issues to closure. The company argues that AI can do real work in these processes, reviewing applications against local code, answering resident questions, flagging violations in plans, and routing inspections.

GovWell says it was founded by the son of a general contractor who watched his father struggle to get permits quickly. Its case for existing is that local governments cannot hire software engineers at competitive salaries. Deployment strategists and configuration tooling are meant to shorten implementations against older systems.

quote.text: Then you try to file a building permit.

AI-powered configuration tools help speed up implementations by 5x compared to legacy solutions

paragraphs: Konveio sells an engagement platform built around planning documents and the full plan lifecycle. The platform is split into an Engagement Hub for public input and a Plan Hub that publishes a Plan Library. Organizations upload materials they already have and take comments on them in place. The company dates its inception to 2020.

Staff can export data to CSV or download annotated PDF reports. Comments from events, letters and emails can be imported and analyzed in one place. The viewer is described as mobile-friendly, WCAG compliant, and screen-reader accessible.

Local Governments are named as an audience, from early stage outreach through implementation stages. State agencies are named for work groups and for drafting policy and legislation. Consultants are named, with plans described as fitting tight budgets or project needs. Colleges, universities and school districts are named for community outreach projects.

quote.text: Konveio's mission is to help community builders get informed buy-in for their efforts to create a better tomorrow.

provenance.quote: Konveio is the Planner’s engagement platform, designed to simplify how communities engage with stakeholders throughout the full plan lifecycle and find answers in their complex framework of guiding documents.

Konveio’s Engagement Hub creates buy-in for planning projects, supporting public input from early stage workshops to draft reviews. And our Plan Hub enables users to publish engaging plans as an AI-connected Plan Library that is ready for questions.
Accept comments on existing materials.
Since its inception in 2020, Konveio has helped community leaders to get buy-in from internal and external stakeholders to drive projects from kick-off through revision, approval, and implementation.
Extract insights quickly. Export your data to CSV or download annotated PDF reports.
Import comments from events, letters, emails or other sources, then analyze everything in one place.
Mobile-friendly, WCAG compliant, and screen-reader accessible.
We empower Local Governments to better connect with their stakeholders, which starts with early stage outreach, ongoing participation, and supports plans through their implementation stages.

We empower agencies to better connect with their stakeholders, facilitate work groups or draft policy and legislation, which starts with early stage collaboration and supports plans through their implementation stages.

We understand the unique needs of planning projects and support consultants with flexible plans that fit into tight budgets or requirements for tailored platforms that support specific client or project needs.

We work with colleges, universities and school districts to support their community outreach, with projects ranging from facility master plans, to Diversity, Equity & Inclusion strategies, and redistricting.

before.source: ICMA 2025; NRPA 2026; ICMA 2026; NLC City Summit 2026; ICC 2026; APA California Chapter 2026

paragraphs: Accela sells software that government agencies use to run permitting, licensing, and asset management from a single system. Its applications are built for individual government service workflows and can operate together or be deployed only where an agency needs them.

For building departments, intake, plan review, inspections, and permit issuance sit in one workflow rather than in separate disconnected steps. Reviewers from different departments work the same record at once, with annotations and approvals tracked as they happen. Planning teams get the same shared review model, plus automated public notice generation, hearing schedules, and agency notifications. Applicants can see where a case stands and receive consolidated feedback from every reviewing department.

The company says it has thirty years of government expertise built into the product. Testimonials on the site are attributed to municipal staff, including a chief building official in McAllen, Texas. Residents and businesses who encounter Accela through a local agency are directed to that agency rather than to the company.

before.buyer: City, county and state government agencies only - 900+ agencies and more than half of the top US cities and counties, with City of McAllen TX, Cabarrus County NC, Manatee County FL, Citrus County FL, City of Rochester MN and City of Charlotte NC named as customers.
before.scope_note: Government-exclusive as far as its own site is concerned. The solutions menu is literally segmented by /solutions/city/, /solutions/county/ and /solutions/state/, and neither the homepage nor the solutions page names a private enterprise, utility or contractor as a buyer. Pure SLED - no federal-only caveat needed. Our 'Permitting & Licensing' category matches what the site sells.
